The main estimating equation is: 𝑌𝑐𝑡 = 𝛼𝑐 + 𝜆𝑡 + 𝛽 (Post𝑡 ∗ Exposure𝑐) + 𝜀𝑐𝑡 (1) where 𝑌𝑐𝑡 is a grade outcome for course c in year t, 𝛼𝑐 is a course fixed effect, 𝜆𝑡 is a year fixed effect, Postt = 1 for t >= 2023, and Exposurec is the share of writing and coding tasks measured from the Fall 2022 syllabus. The coefficient 𝛽 captures the differential post-ChatGPT change in grade outcomes for courses with higher AI task exposure. Standard errors are clustered at the course level throughout; department-level clustering is reported as a robustness check (Table A2). I also estimate a dynamic version of equation (1) by replacing Postt * Exposurec with a full set of year-by-exposure interactions, normalizing to 2022. This produces the event-study figures and is used for the pre-trend tests. The identifying assumption is that, absent ChatGPT’s release, grade trends would have evolved in parallel across high- and low-exposure courses. Several features of the design support this assumption. The exposure measure is constructed from pre-treatment syllabi, removing any possibility of reverse causation. The balanced panel holds course composition fixed across years. I test the assumption using a joint Wald test of the pre-treatment year-by-exposure interactions from the dynamic specification (Table A3). Grade increases in AI-exposed courses are consistent with multiple mechanisms: genuine learning gains through augmentation or reinstatement, sorting of stronger students into exposed courses, or grade inflation through task displacement. As developed in Section 2, these mechanisms have different predictions for where grade increases should be concentrated. Under augmentation/reinstatement or sorting, grades should rise regardless of assessment format. Under displacement, AI can substitute for student effort on take-home work, but is less likely to assist with supervised in-class assessments, so grade increases should be larger in courses where homework carries greater weight. To distinguish between these mechanisms, I augment equation (1) with a triple interaction that exploits variation in homework weight: 15 𝑌𝑐𝑡 = 𝛼𝑐 + 𝜆𝑡 + 𝛽1(Post𝑡 ∗ Exposure𝑐) + 𝛽2(Post𝑡 ∗ HighHW𝑐) + 𝛽3(Post𝑡 ∗ Exposure𝑐 ∗ HighHW𝑐) + 𝜀𝑐𝑡 (2) where HighHWc is an indicator for above-median homework weight (median = 30%), defined from the Fall 2022 cross-section and fixed across years. The coefficient 𝛽1 captures the post- ChatGPT exposure effect in low-homework courses, and 𝛽3 captures the additional effect in high- homework courses. A positive and significant 𝛽3 is consistent with task displacement and difficult to reconcile with augmentation or sorting alone, both of which predict 𝛽3 ≈ 0. I also estimate a dynamic version of equation (2) to examine pre-trends in the triple interaction (Table A12) and produce the event-study figures for the mechanism test (Figure 2). 4 Results 4.1 The Impact of AI Exposure on Grades Figure 1 and corresponding Table A1 present event-study and pooled estimates for cumulative grade thresholds. Pre-treatment coefficients are close to zero and jointly insignificant across all outcomes (Table A3), supporting the parallel trends assumption. After ChatGPT’s release, the share of students receiving an A increased substantially in high-exposure courses, with effects diminishing and becoming insignificant further down the distribution. The pooled estimate for the share of students receiving an A is 13 percentage points, or approximately 30% relative to the 2022 baseline mean of 0.44. The effect becomes smaller and less significant further down the distribution: 9 percentage points for at least A-, 5 percentage points for at least B+, and small and insignificant below that. This pattern is consistent with AI primarily converting A- and B+ grades into A grades, with little effect further down the distribution. 16 Figure 1. The concentration of grade increases in high-homework, high-exposure courses is difficult to reconcile with augmentation or sorting. If AI were improving underlying student skills, those gains should manifest in both homework and exam performance, producing grade increases regardless of assessment format. If stronger students were sorting into high-exposure courses after ChatGPT’s release, that sorting should similarly affect grades across all assessment types. The pattern instead points to task displacement: AI substituting for student effort specifically on the unsupervised assessments where instructors cannot observe the production of submitted work. 4.3 Robustness The main results are robust to alternative exposure definitions, panel construction choices, standard error clustering, and additional controls. The positive effect on the share of A grades and the negative effects on lower grade shares are stable across alternative definitions of AI task exposure (Table A4): all task mentions rather than deduplicated tasks, a binary indicator for any writing or coding task, and writing-only share. Coding-only estimates are directionally similar but less precisely estimated, reflecting the smaller number of coding-intensive courses in the sample. The placebo test using the share of oral 20 presentation tasks yields no significant effects on any grade outcome (Table A7), supporting the interpretation that the results are specific to tasks where AI capabilities are strongest. The results are also insensitive to the panel construction choices. Table A5 shows that the main estimates are stable when varying the minimum enrollment threshold between 15 and 40 students. Table A6 shows that results are unchanged when dropping Fall 2020 and when restricting to a shorter 2021-2025 pre-period, indicating that the COVID-affected semester and the length of the pre-period do not drive the findings. The main estimates remain significant when clustering standard errors at the department rather than the course level (Table A2), and are unchanged when adding instructor stability (the share of Fall 2022 instructors teaching the course in each year) as a time-varying control (Table A8), suggesting that instructor turnover is not confounding the results. The DDD results are similarly robust. The triple interaction coefficient itself is stable when removing 8 courses with imputed homework weights, when using the mean rather than the median as the high-homework threshold, and across stricter enrollment thresholds of 30 and 40 students (Table A13). The triple interaction also remains significant when clustering standard errors at the department level (Table A11). 5 Discussion This paper provides novel evidence that generative AI has become a new mechanism of grade inflation in higher education. I find that courses with higher shares of writing and coding tasks saw substantial grade increases after ChatGPT’s release, accompanied by compression of the grade distribution. These effects are concentrated in courses where homework carries greater assessment weight, consistent with AI substituting for student effort on unsupervised take-home work rather than improving underlying skills. This paper makes three contributions. First, it contributes to the literature on grade inflation by identifying a new mechanism through which grades become distorted signals of student skill. Prior research has documented grade inflation across institutions and identified mechanisms operating through instructor incentives (Langbein 2008; Carrell and West 2010; Keng 2018), signaling competition (Chan et al. 2007), institutional policies (Bar et al. 2012; Butcher et al. 2014), and measurement error and bias (Hanna and Linden 2012; Diamond and Persson 2016). 21 These mechanisms share a common structure: they operate downstream of the production of student work, through how submitted work is evaluated, recorded, or disclosed. Generative AI introduces a fundamentally different channel: it alters the production of graded work itself, before instructors observe and assess it. The resulting distortion is selective rather than uniform, concentrated in courses whose task bundles overlap most strongly with AI capabilities and amplified where assessment relies on unsupervised work. This selectivity has implications beyond the average grade level: it reduces the comparability of grades across courses and potentially across students with unequal access to more capable AI tools, eroding the informational value of transcripts in ways that are difficult to detect from grade distributions alone. Second, the paper contributes to the emerging literature on the impact of generative AI on student achievement. Existing work shows that AI systems perform well on college assessments (Geerling et al. 2023; Borges et al. 2024) and that students increasingly use them for academic work, including to produce graded assignments (Contractor and Reyes 2025). This paper provides evidence that the effects of AI on grades are task-specific, concentrated in courses whose task bundles overlap with AI capabilities, and amplified by assessment formats that give AI the greatest scope to substitute for student effort. It also cautions that measured gains in student performance following AI adoption may reflect shifts in the production of submitted work rather than genuine improvements in underlying skill – a distinction that has direct implications for how AI-era grade data should be interpreted by employers, graduate programs, and researchers studying human capital formation. These findings extend recent evidence from Hausman et al. (2025), who find that AI availability raises grades in courses with home-based assessments, by showing that the effect is driven by task composition rather than assessment format alone. Third, the paper also demonstrates the potential of a task-based approach to study the impact of AI on skill formation in educational settings. While prior work focuses on the impact of AI on production, occupations, and worker productivity (Webb 2019; Eloundou et al. 2024; Brynjolfsson et al. 2025), this paper shows that task-based models also provide a useful framework for understanding how AI operates in educational settings. Applied to higher education, the framework highlights that students develop skills by completing learning tasks, and that AI can affect learning by displacing, augmenting, or reinstating student task practice (Chirikov 2026). The grade- distortion implications documented here follow directly from the displacement mechanism: when 22 AI improves submitted work on assessed tasks without corresponding skill growth, grades become less informative measures of student capability. Several limitations of the study are worth discussing. First, the analysis covers a single institution, which limits external generalizability. However, the findings are consistent with a general mechanism that is not specific to this institution, and the breadth of disciplinary coverage in the sample suggests the results are unlikely to reflect idiosyncratic features of a single field or department. Second, the balanced panel is restricted to courses large enough to appear in the public grade distributions, which may underrepresent small seminars and upper-division courses. Varying the enrollment threshold between 15 and 40 students leaves results unchanged, suggesting this restriction does not drive the findings. Third, the exposure measure captures task composition from syllabi but does not directly measure actual student AI use at the course level. However, prior research showed that courses with higher task exposure are substantially more likely to have adopted explicit AI policies (Chirikov 2026), indicating that instructors in high-exposure courses independently recognized the relevance of AI to their assessments. Fourth, the findings describe average effects across courses and students, but there is likely substantial heterogeneity in how individual students engage with AI that the design cannot capture. Some students may be using AI to substitute for their own effort on graded work, while others may be using it to augment their learning or to practice new AI-related tasks through reinstatement. The aggregate grade increases documented here reflect the net effect of these individual-level differences, and the DDD identifies displacement as the dominant mechanism on average, but the distribution of mechanisms across students within a course remains unobserved. Understanding this heterogeneity requires individual-level data linking student AI use to performance across different assessment formats, which remains an important direction for future research. The findings have implications for the development and allocation of human capital. If grades in writing- and coding-intensive courses increasingly reflect AI-assisted output rather than student skill, employers and graduate programs relying on transcripts for screening and matching decisions may make less efficient allocations, increasing the demand for alternative assessments of core capabilities. Distorted grade signals may also weaken human capital development if students, receiving higher grades, overestimate their mastery and underinvest in foundational skills. More 23 broadly, if AI displaces skill-building tasks during learning, students may graduate with weaker capabilities in precisely the domains where AI is strongest, reinforcing a feedback loop between AI in education and AI in production that could accelerate automation and widen skill gaps in the labor market. Assessment reform is the most direct institutional response, but its design is non-trivial (Corbin et al. 2025). Moving all assessments to supervised in-person environments would limit AI’s scope to substitute for student work, but this approach has important constraints. Not all skills can be meaningfully evaluated under exam conditions: the ability to produce a well-researched essay, develop a software project, or conduct an empirical analysis requires sustained engagement that timed in-person assessments cannot capture. Restricting assessment to formats that are AI- proof risks measuring a narrower set of capabilities than the ones courses are designed to develop, potentially undermining the learning goals that graded work is meant to serve. A more promising direction is to redesign assessments so that AI use is either structurally constrained by the task or purposefully incorporated into it, for example, by requiring students to document their process, justify their choices, or demonstrate understanding through follow-up interaction. The evidence in this paper that instructors in high-exposure courses are already moving toward more explicit AI regulation (Chirikov 2026) suggests that course-level adaptation is underway, but the pace and effectiveness of these responses remain open questions for future research. 24 References 1. ### https://www.dailycal.org/news/campus/academics/uc-berkeley-shows-no-signs-of-ai-grade-inflation-as-professors-adapt/article_6da85b38-889f-4f80-835a-88cc54a81662.html
# UC Berkeley shows no signs of AI grade inflation as professors adapt

A study released by UC Berkeley’s Center for Studies in Higher Education found a correlation between the release of ChatGPT in 2022 and an increased share of A grades for classes with take-home assignments at a selective public university in Texas. However, Berkeleytime data collected by The Daily Californian found no equivalent trends at UC Berkeley.

Between 2019 and spring 2026, A’s at UC Berkeley consistently stayed between 30% and 35%, with a dip during the COVID-19 pandemic likely due to increased pass/no pass courses.

The study, authored by Igor Chirikov, a senior researcher and director of the Student Experience in the Research University Consortium at the Center for Studies in Higher Education, analyzed 500,000 grades from 2018-25 and found that the share of A grades increased by 13 percentage points at the Texas university.

“The pattern shows grades rising mainly where students can use AI on unsupervised take-home work,” Chirikov said in an email. “This strongly suggests that AI is substituting for student effort rather than improving underlying skills.”

While the study found that grades have been increasing in classes with lots of take-home assignments, grades across UC Berkeley have remained relatively stable.

The Daily Cal scraped more than 30,000 course grades beginning in the summer of 2019 from Berkeleytime to assess grade trends at UC Berkeley compared to the university in the study.

Nevertheless, professors across departments on campus have been feeling and responding to the challenges that AI presents to their classrooms.

Josh Hug, a professor in the electrical engineering and computer sciences department, has found that the amount of AI-generated work submitted by students has increased considerably, but said grades have decreased.

In EECS and computer science courses, some classes’ failing grades have [more than doubled](https://www.dailycal.org/news/campus/academics/failing-grades-soar-as-professors-see-greater-ai-usage-dwindling-math-skills-in-uc-berkeley/article_16fad0bf-02cb-4b8c-8d88-888ffd9f8608.html) in the spring 2026 semester. Professors attributed the increase to an increased reliance on AI, a lack of math preparedness and understaffing within classes.

“The reason is that they’re still getting full scores on the assignments, but they’re doing much worse on exams,” Hug said.

To adapt to AI, Hug has been incorporating frequent in-class quizzes, oral check-ins and “diagnostic questions” on exams.

Hug reuses questions from past exams and compares the performance between the two groups of students.

“I have found that students do far worse on these problems than they used to, which is my biggest piece of evidence that they don’t quite know what they’re doing in the way they used to,” Hug said.

History professor Mark Brilliant has run into similar challenges, with students especially struggling with writing.

“Writing is the biggest challenge,” Brilliant said. “Nothing substitutes for writing as a way to develop one’s own voice — one’s intellectual voice.”

In the spring 2026 semester, Brilliant integrated Rumi into his assignments, a platform that allows professors to analyze keystrokes, copy and paste history and potential use of large language models. As a result, he was able to analyze the writing process of students and look for signs of AI.

Michael Mark Cohen, a professor in the American studies and African American studies departments, has similar concerns about students submitting AI-generated papers.

Similar to Hug, Cohen has returned to having more in-person assignments and requirements such as tracking attendance, in-class exams and presentations.

Cohen expressed frustration with the time it takes for both him and his GSIs to sift through papers that use AI. As a result, he has failed “twice as many people” as he did before.

“If you want to cheat, then in the end you’re cheating yourself,” Cohen said. “At some point somewhere down the line, somebody’s going to realize that you paid for a very expensive education and didn’t learn anything.”

## Note's cited sources (verify these)
### https://www.techtimes.com/articles/318817/20260622/ai-grade-inflation-documented-500000-grades-homework-rises-skills-do-not.htm
# AI Grade Inflation Documented in 500,000 Grades: Homework Rises, Skills Do Not

![Illustration picture shows a child doing homework with the Microsoft ](https://d.techtimes.com/en/full/467155/illustration-picture-shows-child-doing-homework-microsoft.jpg?w=836&f=e1ae6df59046062caf919e938230c7a3)

Illustration picture shows a child doing homework with the Microsoft Teams software in Gent, Monday 20 April 2020. Belgium is in its sixth week of confinement in the ongoing corona virus crisis. The measures announced on March 18th in Belgium to avoid the spread of the Covid-19 will remain active until May 4th. BELGA MAG/AFP via Getty Images/JAMES ARTHUR GEKIERE

Princeton University ends its 133-year tradition of unproctored exams on July 1, when human proctors enter campus testing rooms for the first time since 1893. Harvard's faculty voted in May to cap A grades at 20 percent of each class, a limit that takes effect in fall 2027. The two largest academic integrity overhauls at elite universities in a generation share the same cause — and a new study now quantifies it with precision that has been missing from the debate.

Researchers at UC Berkeley analyzed more than 500,000 grades across 319 courses and 84 departments at a large selective public research university in Texas, tracking grade distributions across eight fall semesters from 2018 to 2025. The finding, published May 13 by UC Berkeley's Center for Studies in Higher Education and authored by senior researcher [Igor Chirikov](https://cshe.berkeley.edu/people/igor-chirikov), is difficult to dismiss: in courses with high shares of writing and coding assignments, the proportion of students earning A grades jumped by 13 percentage points after ChatGPT launched — roughly 30 percent above the 2022 baseline. Average GPA rose by 0.12 points, and the grade distribution compressed. Students who previously landed in the A-minus and B-plus range are now earning straight A's.

The effect is not evenly distributed. It is concentrated precisely where AI tools are most useful and hardest to monitor.

### The Homework Signature That Rules Out Better Learning

The study's methodology is what makes its conclusions credible rather than merely suggestive. Chirikov used a difference-in-differences design — a quasi-experimental statistical technique from econometrics that compares grade trajectories across a treatment group and a control group before and after a specific event. The treatment group comprised courses with high AI exposure; the control group comprised courses where AI offers less practical advantage, such as sculpture and laboratory-based science.

The critical design choice was measuring AI exposure using syllabi from fall 2022, before ChatGPT existed publicly. Because course characteristics were assigned before the tool was available, the analysis sidesteps one of the most common confounds in this kind of research: the possibility that instructors who expected to use AI were the ones who redesigned courses to accommodate it. In this study, no instructor could have anticipated ChatGPT when setting fall 2022 course structure.

The parallel trend assumption — the foundational requirement for a valid difference-in-differences result — holds here: before November 2022, AI-exposed and non-exposed courses showed similar grade trajectories. The divergence begins precisely when ChatGPT became widely available and sharpened each subsequent semester.

Chirikov then tested the learning hypothesis directly. If AI tools genuinely improved student understanding, grade gains should appear across all assessments — including proctored in-class exams where AI cannot be used. If AI is instead substituting for unsupervised take-home work, gains should concentrate in courses where homework carries greater weight in the final grade.

The data delivered a clear answer. In courses where homework exceeded the median share of the final grade, the A-grade share rose by an additional 16 percentage points compared to similarly AI-exposed courses that weighted exams more heavily. In lower-homework courses, the post-ChatGPT grade effect was small and statistically insignificant.

A placebo test reinforced the conclusion. For oral presentation assignments — where AI offers little practical advantage — grades showed no meaningful change after ChatGPT's release. Chirikov describes the combined pattern as "difficult to reconcile with broad learning gains or sorting effects alone."

### When AI Does Homework, Grades Change Before Instructors Even Grade

Prior research attributed the decades-long rise in American university grades to teaching evaluation incentives, competition between institutions, and grading leniency policies. Harvard's share of A grades climbed from 24 percent in 2005 to 60.2 percent in 2025, the study notes. But all of those earlier mechanisms operated at the grading stage — instructors awarding higher marks after students submitted their work.

AI introduces a structurally different mechanism. It changes the work itself before an instructor evaluates it. A student who submits an AI-generated essay has not triggered a grading decision that inflates the result; the submitted work genuinely looks like A-quality material to the instructor reading it. The grade is accurate given what the instructor sees. What the instructor cannot see is that the work does not reflect what the student knows how to do.

This distinction matters for which solutions can work. Policies that target instructor leniency — Harvard's grade cap, grade normalization policies — address the symptom rather than the production mechanism. Proctored in-class exams address the mechanism directly, which is why Princeton's move to universal exam supervision is more structurally targeted than Harvard's grade-capping approach. Neither is sufficient on its own.

The scale of the commercial ecosystem supporting AI-assisted homework submission reflects the demand. At least 150 AI "humanizer" tools now exist specifically to rewrite AI-generated text so it evades detection software. [NBC News](https://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/national-international/avoid-accusations-ai-cheating-college-students-ai/6451208/) reported in January 2026 that 43 such platforms drew a combined 33.9 million website visits in October, with some charging up to $50 a month. These tools operate by manipulating the two primary signals that AI detection software analyzes — perplexity (how statistically predictable the text is) and burstiness (how much sentence length varies) — to mimic the irregular patterns of human prose. Turnitin, the leading academic plagiarism detection service, has acknowledged that its AI detection model "may not always be accurate."

### What Employers and Graduate Programs Are About to Discover

For a credential to carry economic value, the grade must correlate with what a graduate can actually do. In economist Michael Spence's foundational [signaling model of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signalling_\(economics\)), the information value of a credential depends on it being differentially costly to obtain — meaning that students with stronger underlying ability can achieve it at lower cost than weaker students, creating a gap that makes the credential informative to an observer who cannot directly measure ability. When AI collapses the cost of producing A-grade work to near zero across the ability spectrum, that separating condition breaks down. The grade no longer reliably separates those who developed the relevant skill from those who did not.

Employers appear to be registering this shift. Recruiting platforms that track employer GPA requirements report rising minimum thresholds as companies try to filter out inflated credentials, a response that perversely penalizes students who earned high grades legitimately, because their transcripts are no longer distinguishable from those of students who outsourced the work.

Chirikov flags a feedback loop with consequences that extend beyond the hiring stage. If AI handles the assignments meant to build writing and coding competencies during college, graduates could emerge weaker in precisely the skills AI is most capable of substituting in the workplace. That dynamic — AI-weakened human workers creating demand for more AI substitution — could accelerate automation pressure on entry-level roles in knowledge industries.

The pattern appeared in stark form at UC Berkeley's own Computer Science department in spring 2026. The student newspaper [The Daily Californian](https://www.dailycal.org/news/campus/academics/failing-grades-soar-as-professors-see-greater-ai-usage-dwindling-math-skills-in-uc-berkeley/article_16fad0bf-02cb-4b8c-8d88-888ffd9f8608.html) reported failure rates of 35 percent in CS 10 and 10.6 percent in CS 61A — both figures far above the department's stated norms. Teaching professor Dan Garcia described the "primary driver" as a "vast increase in academic dishonesty due to students' usage of large language models." Students had submitted polished AI-generated homework across the semester and then encountered proctored in-class exams they had not prepared to pass.

### Even OpenAI Sees the Skills Atrophy Risk

OpenAI chief executive [Sam Altman](https://the-decoder.com/ai-is-inflating-student-grades-and-the-effect-points-to-outsourced-work-not-better-learning/) acknowledged in a recent interview that three and a half years after ChatGPT's launch, the education system had responded far less than he expected. He had anticipated a brief period of disruption followed by meaningful institutional reform. Instead, he said he could point to no systemic change. Without one, Altman warned, critical thinking skills risk "significant atrophy."

"I'm someone who thinks through writing, and I write a lot of things I never show anyone, but it's still important to me for figuring things out," Altman said. "That's why I'm grateful that I learned to write. People say the same thing about programming." Both skills, he argued, train the mind independent of their practical outputs — and both are exactly the skills that AI currently handles with the greatest ease.

The concern is not hypothetical. A March 2026 [National Bureau of Economic Research working paper](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34952) by economists Jeffrey Denning, Rachel Nesbit, Nolan Pope, and Merrill Warnick found that exposure to higher average grade inflation — even prior to AI — reduced students' long-term earnings by an estimated $213,872 in present value per student affected by each additional standard deviation of inflated grading. Students who received inflated grades were less likely to pass subsequent courses, showed lower test scores, and enrolled in college at lower rates. AI-driven grade inflation operates through the same mechanism but at greater speed and scale.

### What Needs to Change in How Universities Assess Students

The Berkeley study stops short of recommending a return to universally proctored in-person exams, noting that approach is neither sufficient nor straightforward to implement across a full curriculum. Chirikov instead recommends redesigning assessments to either constrain AI use through process-oriented formats or integrate it explicitly in ways that still verify student understanding. Options include requiring documentation of a work process, or conducting follow-up interactions — oral or written — that confirm a student can explain and extend what they submitted.

The approach parallels policy steps already taken elsewhere. Norway restricted generative AI tools in elementary schools and limited their use in secondary schools in 2026, with Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere citing concern that uncritical AI use allows students to skip foundational learning steps. A May 2026 [Cornell-led study](https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2026/05/widespread-ai-misuse-means-higher-ed-must-rethink-assessment) surveying more than 95,000 students at 20 research universities found that approximately one-third used generative AI regularly in completing assignments, and 9 percent had used it to cheat. Cornell information science professor Rene Kizilcec, a study co-author, called assessment reform "necessary and urgent," warning that AI misuse threatens "the credibility of university credentials."

Princeton's proctoring shift, effective July 1, addresses the homework-to-exam gap in the most direct way available: any grade a student earns on a supervised exam is now free from AI substitution, regardless of what happened on take-home assignments. Harvard's grade cap takes a different approach, imposing a limit on A-grade frequency that constrains grade inflation at the output stage. Chirikov observed to [The Boston Globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/05/20/metro/harvard-votes-to-limit-as/) that Harvard's cap does not address the underlying mechanism: "AI helps produce the work being graded, so the question really is, 'Do grades still tell us what students can actually do?'"

Fifty percent of U.S. higher education institutions still lack formal AI policies, according to Coursera's 2026 data. In that environment, the Berkeley study provides the clearest empirical evidence to date that the absence of institutional response is not benign — it has a measurable, quantifiable effect on what a college grade means, and by extension on what a college diploma certifies to everyone who relies on it.

* * *

### Frequently Asked Questions

**What does the Berkeley AI grade inflation study show?**

A UC Berkeley study analyzing more than 500,000 grades from 2018 to 2025 found that courses heavy on writing and coding assignments saw a 13-percentage-point increase in A grades after ChatGPT launched in late 2022 — about 30 percent above the pre-AI baseline. The increase was concentrated in courses where homework carried greater weight in the final grade, and did not appear in oral presentation assignments, suggesting students are using AI to complete take-home work rather than genuinely learning more.

**Does AI cheating actually affect college grades at scale?**

Yes. The Berkeley study uses a difference-in-differences econometric design — one of the most rigorous methods available for causal inference in observational data — to isolate AI's effect from other explanations. The study's key design feature is that AI exposure was measured using syllabi from fall 2022, before ChatGPT existed, ruling out the possibility that instructors redesigned courses in response to AI. The 13-percentage-point spike is causal, not merely correlational.

**Why can't AI detection tools solve the ChatGPT homework cheating problem?**

AI detection software analyzes statistical patterns in text — primarily perplexity (how predictable the text is) and burstiness (how much sentence length varies) — to identify machine-generated writing. A commercial ecosystem of at least 150 "humanizer" tools now exists specifically to rewrite AI-generated text in ways that evade detection by manipulating those signals. Turnitin has acknowledged its detection model may produce inaccurate results. Research has also shown that detection tools disproportionately flag writing by non-native English speakers. The Berkeley study's value is precisely that it does not rely on detection — it measures grade patterns at scale, making the finding robust to whatever evasion technology students use.

**What can universities do to restore the academic integrity AI has compromised?**

The most structurally targeted response is redesigning assessments to require verified student understanding — proctored in-class exams, oral follow-up interviews, documented work processes, or AI-integrated assignments that still demand students explain their reasoning. Princeton's move to universal exam proctoring beginning July 1 directly closes the homework gap the Berkeley study identified. Harvard's grade cap addresses output rather than cause. Norway has restricted generative AI use in elementary and secondary schools. The Berkeley study's author argues there is no single solution but that institutions must invest more heavily in assessment reform than most have done in the three and a half years since ChatGPT's release.

### https://www.dailycal.org/news/campus/academics/uc-berkeley-shows-no-signs-of-ai-grade-inflation-as-professors-adapt/article_6da85b38-889f-4f80-835a-88cc54a81662.html
# UC Berkeley shows no signs of AI grade inflation as professors adapt

A study released by UC Berkeley’s Center for Studies in Higher Education found a correlation between the release of ChatGPT in 2022 and an increased share of A grades for classes with take-home assignments at a selective public university in Texas. However, Berkeleytime data collected by The Daily Californian found no equivalent trends at UC Berkeley.

Between 2019 and spring 2026, A’s at UC Berkeley consistently stayed between 30% and 35%, with a dip during the COVID-19 pandemic likely due to increased pass/no pass courses.

The study, authored by Igor Chirikov, a senior researcher and director of the Student Experience in the Research University Consortium at the Center for Studies in Higher Education, analyzed 500,000 grades from 2018-25 and found that the share of A grades increased by 13 percentage points at the Texas university.

“The pattern shows grades rising mainly where students can use AI on unsupervised take-home work,” Chirikov said in an email. “This strongly suggests that AI is substituting for student effort rather than improving underlying skills.”

While the study found that grades have been increasing in classes with lots of take-home assignments, grades across UC Berkeley have remained relatively stable.

The Daily Cal scraped more than 30,000 course grades beginning in the summer of 2019 from Berkeleytime to assess grade trends at UC Berkeley compared to the university in the study.

Nevertheless, professors across departments on campus have been feeling and responding to the challenges that AI presents to their classrooms.

Josh Hug, a professor in the electrical engineering and computer sciences department, has found that the amount of AI-generated work submitted by students has increased considerably, but said grades have decreased.

In EECS and computer science courses, some classes’ failing grades have [more than doubled](https://www.dailycal.org/news/campus/academics/failing-grades-soar-as-professors-see-greater-ai-usage-dwindling-math-skills-in-uc-berkeley/article_16fad0bf-02cb-4b8c-8d88-888ffd9f8608.html) in the spring 2026 semester. Professors attributed the increase to an increased reliance on AI, a lack of math preparedness and understaffing within classes.

“The reason is that they’re still getting full scores on the assignments, but they’re doing much worse on exams,” Hug said.

To adapt to AI, Hug has been incorporating frequent in-class quizzes, oral check-ins and “diagnostic questions” on exams.

Hug reuses questions from past exams and compares the performance between the two groups of students.

“I have found that students do far worse on these problems than they used to, which is my biggest piece of evidence that they don’t quite know what they’re doing in the way they used to,” Hug said.

History professor Mark Brilliant has run into similar challenges, with students especially struggling with writing.

“Writing is the biggest challenge,” Brilliant said. “Nothing substitutes for writing as a way to develop one’s own voice — one’s intellectual voice.”

In the spring 2026 semester, Brilliant integrated Rumi into his assignments, a platform that allows professors to analyze keystrokes, copy and paste history and potential use of large language models. As a result, he was able to analyze the writing process of students and look for signs of AI.

Michael Mark Cohen, a professor in the American studies and African American studies departments, has similar concerns about students submitting AI-generated papers.

Similar to Hug, Cohen has returned to having more in-person assignments and requirements such as tracking attendance, in-class exams and presentations.

Cohen expressed frustration with the time it takes for both him and his GSIs to sift through papers that use AI. As a result, he has failed “twice as many people” as he did before.

“If you want to cheat, then in the end you’re cheating yourself,” Cohen said. “At some point somewhere down the line, somebody’s going to realize that you paid for a very expensive education and didn’t learn anything.”

### https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/remaining-jewish-population-of-europe-in-1945
# Jewish Population of Europe in 1945 | Holocaust Encyclopedia

\[caption=374377e9-1f14-4ad7-9840-8766e6d1276d\] - \[credit=374377e9-1f14-4ad7-9840-8766e6d1276d\]

Approximately 9.5 million Jews lived in Europe in 1933, the year Hitler came to power. This number represented 1.7% of Europe's total population and more than 60 percent of the world's Jewish population. By 1945, most European Jews—2 out of every 3—had been killed.

*   ![](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/images/large/01d76c58-c56a-4c97-bb54-8e350f9cf321.gif)
    
    [European Jewish population distribution, ca. 1933](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/map/european-jewish-population-distribution-ca-1933)
    
    Jews have lived in Europe for more than two thousand years. The American Jewish Yearbook placed the total [Jewish population of Europe](/narrative/2906/en) at about 9.5 million in 1933. This number represented more than 60 percent of the world's Jewish population, which was estimated at 15.3 million. Most European Jews resided in eastern Europe, with about 5 1/2 million Jews living in Poland and the Soviet Union. Before the [Nazi takeover of power](/narrative/65/en) in 1933, Europe had a dynamic and highly developed Jewish culture. In little more than a decade, most of Europe would be conquered, occupied, or annexed by [Nazi Germany](/narrative/2529/en) and most European Jews—[two out of every three](/narrative/11652/en)—would be dead.
    
*   ![](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/images/large/7ee11f56-7c91-4648-80f4-853a8c3163a9.gif)

Six million Jews died in the [Holocaust](/narrative/72/en). Jewish communities across Europe were shattered. Many of those who survived were determined to leave Europe and start new lives in Israel or the United States. The population shifts brought on by the Holocaust and by Jewish emigration were astounding.

According to the _American Jewish Yearbook_, the Jewish population of Europe was about 9.5 million in [1933](/narrative/2906/en). In 1950, the Jewish population of Europe was about 3.5 million. In 1933, 60 percent of all Jews lived in Europe. In 1950, most Jews (51 percent) lived in the Americas (North and South combined), while only a third of the world's Jewish population lived in Europe.

The Jewish communities of eastern Europe were devastated. In 1933, Poland had the largest Jewish population in Europe, numbering over three million. By 1950, the Jewish population of Poland was reduced to about 45,000. The Soviet Union had the largest remaining Jewish population, with some two million Jews. Romania's Jewish population was nearly 757,000 in 1930 and fell to approximately 280,000 (1950). Most of these demographic losses were due to the Holocaust, the rest to postwar emigration from Europe.

![Klara Taussig and Ernst Brecher go on an outing in the Austrian countryside before their marriage.](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/images/large/173f8937-0e52-4aee-846d-508eed4e4249.jpg)

Klara Taussig and Ernst Brecher go on an outing in the Austrian countryside before their marriage. They later had a son, Heinz, who was born on August 29, 1932 in Graz, Austria. where his father was a merchant. After the [Germans annexed Austria](/narrative/64610/en) in 1938, Klara and Ernst sent Heinz to live with friends of an aunt in Zagreb.

Heinz survived and eventually came to the United States on the _Henry Gibbins_, a military troop transport. Klara and Ernst died in the [concentration camps](/narrative/2689/en). 

Photograph taken in Austria, 1930–32. 

Credits:

*   US Holocaust Memorial Museum, courtesy of Henry H. Brecher

The Jewish population of central Europe was also devastated. Germany had a Jewish population of 525,000 in 1933 and just 37,000 in 1950. Hungary had 445,000 in 1933 and 190,000 in 1950. Czechoslovakia's Jewish population was reduced from about 357,000 in 1933 to 17,000 in 1950 and Austria's from about 191,000 to just 18,000.

In western Europe, the largest Jewish communities remained in Great Britain, with approximately 450,000 Jews (300,000 in 1933) and France, with 235,000 (250,000 in 1933). In southern Europe, the Jewish population fell dramatically: in Greece from about 73,000 in 1933 to just 7,000 in 1950; in Yugoslavia from about 70,000 to 3,500; in Italy from about 48,000 to 35,000; and in Bulgaria from 50,000 in 1933 to just 6,500 in 1950 (the reduction in the Bulgarian Jewish population resulted from postwar emigration). The demographic focus of European Jewry thus shifted from eastern to western Europe.

Before the [Nazi takeover of power](/narrative/65/en) in 1933, Europe had a vibrant and mature Jewish culture. By 1945, most European Jews—two out of every three—had been killed. Most of the surviving remnant of European Jewry decided to leave Europe. Hundreds of thousands established new lives in Israel, the United States, Canada, Australia, Great Britain, South America, and South Africa.

> And we were traveling criss-cross Poland looking for surviving Jews, and we found them. And sometimes these meetings were so packed with emotion that I, I lack the words to describe it, you know. Because the idea that we are really survivors couldn't sink in yet.   
> —Leah Hammerstein Silverstein

  Your browser does not support this video element. Please consider using a more recent web browser.

Leah grew up in Praga, a suburb of Warsaw, Poland. She was active in the Ha-Shomer ha-Tsa'ir Zionist youth movement. Germany [invaded Poland](/narrative/2103/en) in September 1939. Jews were forced to live in the [Warsaw](/narrative/2014/en) ghetto, which the Germans sealed off in November 1940. In the ghetto, Leah lived with a group of Ha-Shomer ha-Tsa'ir members. In September 1941, she and other members of the youth group escaped from the ghetto to a Ha-Shomer ha-Tsa'ir farm in Zarki, near Czestochowa, Poland. In May 1942, Leah became a courier for the underground, using false Polish papers and traveling between the [Krakow](/narrative/3055/en) ghetto and the nearby Plaszow camp. As conditions worsened, she escaped to Tarnow, but soon decided to return to Krakow. Leah also posed as a non-Jewish Pole in Czestochowa and Warsaw, and was a courier for the Jewish National Committee and the Jewish Fighting Organization (ZOB). She fought with a Jewish unit in the Armia Ludowa (People's Army) during the [Warsaw Polish uprising](/narrative/55299/en) in 1944. Leah was liberated by Soviet forces. After the war she helped people emigrate from Poland, then moved to Israel herself before settling in the United States.

# Jewish Population of Europe in 1945 | Holocaust Encyclopedia

\[caption=374377e9-1f14-4ad7-9840-8766e6d1276d\] - \[credit=374377e9-1f14-4ad7-9840-8766e6d1276d\]

Approximately 9.5 million Jews lived in Europe in 1933, the year Hitler came to power. This number represented 1.7% of Europe's total population and more than 60 percent of the world's Jewish population. By 1945, most European Jews—2 out of every 3—had been killed.

*   ![](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/images/large/01d76c58-c56a-4c97-bb54-8e350f9cf321.gif)
    
    [European Jewish population distribution, ca. 1933](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/map/european-jewish-population-distribution-ca-1933)
    
    Jews have lived in Europe for more than two thousand years. The American Jewish Yearbook placed the total [Jewish population of Europe](/narrative/2906/en) at about 9.5 million in 1933. This number represented more than 60 percent of the world's Jewish population, which was estimated at 15.3 million. Most European Jews resided in eastern Europe, with about 5 1/2 million Jews living in Poland and the Soviet Union. Before the [Nazi takeover of power](/narrative/65/en) in 1933, Europe had a dynamic and highly developed Jewish culture. In little more than a decade, most of Europe would be conquered, occupied, or annexed by [Nazi Germany](/narrative/2529/en) and most European Jews—[two out of every three](/narrative/11652/en)—would be dead.
    
*   ![](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/images/large/7ee11f56-7c91-4648-80f4-853a8c3163a9.gif)

Six million Jews died in the [Holocaust](/narrative/72/en). Jewish communities across Europe were shattered. Many of those who survived were determined to leave Europe and start new lives in Israel or the United States. The population shifts brought on by the Holocaust and by Jewish emigration were astounding.

According to the _American Jewish Yearbook_, the Jewish population of Europe was about 9.5 million in [1933](/narrative/2906/en). In 1950, the Jewish population of Europe was about 3.5 million. In 1933, 60 percent of all Jews lived in Europe. In 1950, most Jews (51 percent) lived in the Americas (North and South combined), while only a third of the world's Jewish population lived in Europe.

The Jewish communities of eastern Europe were devastated. In 1933, Poland had the largest Jewish population in Europe, numbering over three million. By 1950, the Jewish population of Poland was reduced to about 45,000. The Soviet Union had the largest remaining Jewish population, with some two million Jews. Romania's Jewish population was nearly 757,000 in 1930 and fell to approximately 280,000 (1950). Most of these demographic losses were due to the Holocaust, the rest to postwar emigration from Europe.

After the [Germans annexed Austria](/narrative/64610/en) in 1938, Klara and Ernst sent Heinz to live with friends of an aunt in Zagreb.

Heinz survived and eventually came to the United States on the _Henry Gibbins_, a military troop transport. Klara and Ernst died in the [concentration camps](/narrative/2689/en). 

Photograph taken in Austria, 1930–32.

Before the [Nazi takeover of power](/narrative/65/en) in 1933, Europe had a vibrant and mature Jewish culture. By 1945, most European Jews—two out of every three—had been killed. Most of the surviving remnant of European Jewry decided to leave Europe. Hundreds of thousands established new lives in Israel, the United States, Canada, Australia, Great Britain, South America, and South Africa.

> And we were traveling criss-cross Poland looking for surviving Jews, and we found them. And sometimes these meetings were so packed with emotion that I, I lack the words to describe it, you know. Because the idea that we are really survivors couldn't sink in yet.

samples.research:
The claim is misleading. 'It' is almost certainly Lighthaven, the former Rose Garden Inn in Berkeley. The excerpt doesn't name it, so I inferred this from context. Reporting supports only a much narrower version of the claim than the article's wording suggests.

What the sources support:
- The FTX estate's bankruptcy complaint alleges two $500,000 payments. FTX Foundation caused them to be wired from a North Dimension account to a title company on July 13 and Aug 18, 2022. They were an initial deposit for CFAR subsidiary Lightcone RG's purchase of the Rose Garden Inn. The complaint says the transfers were intended as a loan to be repaid once financing closed, and that the debtors' records show no repayment. Lightcone RG closed on the purchase around Nov 4, 2022. This is quoted in the EA Forum post: https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties
- SFGate reports that the FTX lawyers wrote that FTX Foundation sent $1M as an initial deposit and wasn't paid back: https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php

What contradicts or undercuts the claim:
- These were allegations in a complaint, not established findings.
- Lightcone CEO Oliver Habryka stated 'No FTX funds were used in the purchase of Lighthaven.' He posted the escrow company's closing statement. He said the deposit never entered Lightcone's account and was credited and debited from North Dimension Inc, resulting in no equity. Source (the first tweet in the thread, shown on the page): https://x.com/ohabryka/status/1802563860819566701
- SFGate says Habryka posted a screenshot of a 2022 escrow document. It said $1M would be returned to the FTX-linked North Dimension. Habryka guessed the escrow company still held the funds and said 'we never had any of it.' Habryka said the $16.5M purchase price was money Lightcone borrowed from a company owned by Jaan Tallinn: https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php
- A Substack excerpt says the balance of the purchase price, totalling $20M, came via Slimrock Investments. Habryka said Slimrock is controlled by Jaan Tallinn: https://davidzmorris.substack.com/p/a-lever-long-enough-draft-excerpt
- The EA Forum post says Habryka's thread called out the Guardian's claim as inaccurate, and that Vox's Kelsey Piper called the claim a 'really, really bad mistake'. The same post's commenter argued the Guardian was reporting allegations from a public court complaint: https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties
- Habryka wrote that 'FTX never gave us money directly for Lighthaven.' He also said Lightcone did receive other FTX Future Fund funding, and that Tallinn and SFC helped fund the $1.7M settlement with the FTX estate: https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/5n2ZQcbc7r4R8mvqc/the-lightcone-is-nothing-without-its-people

Timing: the two $500K wires were in July and August 2022. That was before FTX's early-November 2022 collapse, and the purchase closed around Nov 4. The 'wired as it was collapsing' framing is therefore questionable.

Conclusion: stating flatly that Lighthaven was 'originally purchased with money wired to CFAR from FTX as it was collapsing' overstates a disputed allegation. The main financing was a Tallinn-linked loan. The FTX-linked $1M was an escrow deposit that Lightcone says it never received and that was to be returned to North Dimension.

## Note's cited sources (verify these)
### https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties

# [Linkpost] Sam Bankman-Fried funded a group with racist ties. FTX wants its $5m back

Comments

21

Sorted by

New & upvoted

33

As others have noted, it looks like the journalists got a lot of basic things wrong in this reporting. I'm doubly frustrated by this because basically all of the EA/rationalist discourse on Twitter is about these mistakes, with almost no discussion of the unchallenged allegations in the piece: that Manifold's conference had attendees/speakers with ties to eugenicist and racist people and groups. 

For example, whether or not Richard Hanania uses prediction markets, I want him nowhere near EA or EA-funded groups/events. For why, [see this](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hanania#Writing_as_%22Richard_Hoste%22_\(2008%E2%80%93early_2010s\)). 

7

> that Manifold's conference had **attendees**/speakers with ties to eugenicist and racist people and groups. 

I think it's somewhat fair to criticize Manifold for their selection of speakers (though I would be hesitant to infer endorsement). 

But I think it's pretty unfair to criticize Manifold for attendees who bought tickets for an event that anyone in the world can buy tickets to. I agree that in as much as any substantial fraction (like idk >10%) of an event ends up full of people who take harmful actions, then that makes sense to be concerned about, but there were 600 people at Manifest, and so I don't think finding a few attendees who have harmful effects on society and the world is much evidence about Manifest.

14

People are notoriously bad at assessing these things, so do take this with a major grain of salt: I would believe >10% of the people present were HBD curious or would endorse and partake in discussions around HBD. If we want better data a survey could be sent to the participants.

4

Oh, I would totally partake in discussions around HBD. In as much as people consider that a harmful action, I strongly disapprove. I think a lot of the claims around it are bunk, and disagree with many people in the space, but I would totally talk to people about it, as I am willing to talk to people about almost everything.

2

This is helpful context. I think it is still a bit unsettling that there was a noticeable strain of this type of stuff from the attendees (like if I went to a ticketed party and noticed that 5% of it was into race science somehow, I'd feel uncomfortable and want to leave.)

5

It's probably good to note that Manifold is not an EA organisation, and Manifest (iiuc) was not funded by EA funders or branded as an EA event (though I think Manifest was trying to channel some of the EA vibe, and many attendees were involved in EA in some way).

8

This is helpful, though Lighthaven is definitely backed by EA money. 

14

Lighthaven will generally rent the space to whoever pays us enough money to make it worth it (and we made on-net money on Manifest, even taking into account staff time), barring some very exceptional circumstances. 

I do think overall Manifest was great and I would subsidize it, but I want to set clear expectations that I absolutely do not endorse everyone who rents space from us (like, I think there is a substantial chance we will host team retreats for capability teams at AI scaling labs, and there is basically no group of people whose actions I condemn more than them, but I still think it's the right choice to rent space to them).

30

25

To be fair to the Guardian, the article is citing those allegations to the complaint filed against Lightcone and related entities in bankruptcy court.

Here are relevant quotes from the complaint (click [here](https://restructuring.ra.kroll.com/FTX/Home-DocketInfo) and search for 24-50066)

> \[para 43\] ... This address is the location of the Rose Garden Inn, a hotel purchased by Lightcone RG in the fall of 2022, in part using funds received from FTX Foundation.
> 
> \[para 47\] On July 13, 2022, and August 18, 2022, FTX Foundation caused payments of $500,000 each to be wired from an account held by North Dimension to a title company as an initial deposit for Lightcone RG’s acquisition of the Rose Garden Inn. Lightcone RG closed on the purchase of the hotel on or about November 4, 2022. Although these transfers were intended as a loan to be re-paid once the financing for the Rose Garden Inn closed, the Debtors records do not indicate that CFAR or Lightcone ever repaid this $1 million “loan.”
> 
> \[para 49\] On October 3, 2022, FTX Foundation approved a grant of $1,500,000 to Lightcone, stipulating that the funds “must be spent for charitable purposes to support the project ‘General Support for Lightcone.’” The grant was paid in a series of 10 transfers made on October 3, 2022 from an account held by FTX Foundation. Upon information and belief, a material portion of the transfers was used by CFAR to fund Lightcone and the acquisition and renovation of the Rose Garden Inn.

\[Note: Upon information and belief is lawyer-speak for _we are guessing that_ . . . . But that's usually considered OK in the context of a complaint, because the plaintiff hasn't had a chance to dig through the defendant's records, depose their officers, and otherwise prove up their case.\]

Turning to the article:

> But that in the months before the collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s [FTX](https://www.theguardian.com/business/ftx) crypto empire, he and other company insiders funnelled almost $5m to Lightcone, including $1m for a deposit to lock in the Rose Garden deal.
> 
> On 13 July and 18 August 2022, _according to the complaint,_ the FTX Foundation also wired two payments of $500,000 each to a title company as a deposit for Lightcone RG’s purchase of the Rose Garden Inn. The complaint says these were intended as a loan but there is no evidence that the $1m was repaid.
> 
> Then, on 3 October, the FTX Foundation approved a $1.5m grant to Lightcone Infrastructure, _according to FTX trustees._
> 
> _The complaint alleges_ that Lightcone got another $20m loan to fund the Rose Garden Inn purchase from Slimrock Investments Pte Ltd, a Singapore-incorporated company owned by Estonian software billionaire, Skype inventor and EA/rationalism adherent Jaan Tallinn. This included the $16.5m purchase price and $3.5m for renovations and repairs.

(emphases mine).

These statements seem at least generally consistent with the complaint at first glance. Could someone point out where they are not?

I think it's generally fair for media outlets to report what is being alleged in complaints filed in litigation of public importance. This isn't a self-represented person alleging that the U.S. government is holding Elvis captive. This is a serious adversary complaint by a serious law firm, that is subject to the norms and sanctions of [Bankruptcy Rule 8011](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frbp/rule_8011). 

The complaint may be wrong, of course -- many complaints ultimately are show to be, or are at least shown to be unproven. But money is fungible, it is undisputed that one transfer from an FTX source was somehow related to the Rose Garden Inn, and it it appears that at least some significant FTX funding was legally unrestricted. I do not think the Guardian was obliged not to report the allegations because Lightcone denied them, nor was it obliged to conduct a forensic audit of Lightcone's books before reporting on what was alleged in a public court complaint.

I believe the estate has a strategic litigation reason for claiming that FTX money was involved with the RG Inn, and so I would temper any credence in the allegations in light of that angle. But what's sauce for the goose is for the gander as well -- Lightcone may have a countervailing strategic litigation reason for denying a connection.

## Research findings (background — not a source)
The claim is misleading. 'It' is almost certainly Lighthaven, the former Rose Garden Inn in Berkeley. The excerpt doesn't name it, so I inferred this from context. Reporting supports only a much narrower version of the claim than the article's wording suggests.

What the sources support:
- The FTX estate's bankruptcy complaint alleges two $500,000 payments. FTX Foundation caused them to be wired from a North Dimension account to a title company on July 13 and Aug 18, 2022. They were an initial deposit for CFAR subsidiary Lightcone RG's purchase of the Rose Garden Inn. The complaint says the transfers were intended as a loan to be repaid once financing closed, and that the debtors' records show no repayment. Lightcone RG closed on the purchase around Nov 4, 2022. This is quoted in the EA Forum post: https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties
- SFGate reports that the FTX lawyers wrote that FTX Foundation sent $1M as an initial deposit and wasn't paid back: https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php

What contradicts or undercuts the claim:
- These were allegations in a complaint, not established findings.
- Lightcone CEO Oliver Habryka stated 'No FTX funds were used in the purchase of Lighthaven.' He posted the escrow company's closing statement. He said the deposit never entered Lightcone's account and was credited and debited from North Dimension Inc, resulting in no equity. Source (the first tweet in the thread, shown on the page): https://x.com/ohabryka/status/1802563860819566701
- SFGate says Habryka posted a screenshot of a 2022 escrow document. It said $1M would be returned to the FTX-linked North Dimension. Habryka guessed the escrow company still held the funds and said 'we never had any of it.' Habryka said the $16.5M purchase price was money Lightcone borrowed from a company owned by Jaan Tallinn: https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php
- A Substack excerpt says the balance of the purchase price, totalling $20M, came via Slimrock Investments. Habryka said Slimrock is controlled by Jaan Tallinn: https://davidzmorris.substack.com/p/a-lever-long-enough-draft-excerpt
- The EA Forum post says Habryka's thread called out the Guardian's claim as inaccurate, and that Vox's Kelsey Piper called the claim a 'really, really bad mistake'. The same post's commenter argued the Guardian was reporting allegations from a public court complaint: https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties
- Habryka wrote that 'FTX never gave us money directly for Lighthaven.' He also said Lightcone did receive other FTX Future Fund funding, and that Tallinn and SFC helped fund the $1.7M settlement with the FTX estate: https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/5n2ZQcbc7r4R8mvqc/the-lightcone-is-nothing-without-its-people

Timing: the two $500K wires were in July and August 2022. That was before FTX's early-November 2022 collapse, and the purchase closed around Nov 4. The 'wired as it was collapsing' framing is therefore questionable.

Conclusion: stating flatly that Lighthaven was 'originally purchased with money wired to CFAR from FTX as it was collapsing' overstates a disputed allegation. The main financing was a Tallinn-linked loan. The FTX-linked $1M was an escrow deposit that Lightcone says it never received and that was to be returned to North Dimension.

I think it's generally fair for media outlets to report what is being alleged in complaints filed in litigation of public importance. This isn't a self-represented person alleging that the U.S. government is holding Elvis captive. This is a serious adversary complaint by a serious law firm, that is subject to the norms and sanctions of [Bankruptcy Rule 8011](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frbp/rule_8011). 

The complaint may be wrong, of course -- many complaints ultimately are show to be, or are at least shown to be unproven. But money is fungible, it is undisputed that one transfer from an FTX source was somehow related to the Rose Garden Inn, and it it appears that at least some significant FTX funding was legally unrestricted. ## Research findings (background — not a source)
The claim is misleading. "It" appears to be the Rose Garden Inn in Berkeley, now Lighthaven, though the excerpt doesn't name it. I am restating my earlier findings without running a new search. Two of the sources below, the EA Forum linkpost and the SFGATE article, are the ones I cited before, and I have not re-verified their text here.

1. What the lawsuit alleges. The FTX estate's complaint says that in the months before the November 2022 collapse, insiders sent almost $5M to Lightcone, including $1M as a deposit to lock in the Rose Garden deal (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties). The complaint also alleges that CFAR used other FTX Foundation grant money to buy and renovate the property (https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php). These are allegations, not findings.

2. Timing. The transfers came months before the collapse. They did not come "as it was collapsing", as the claim says.

3. Where the money went. Lightcone's CEO told SFGATE that the $1M went to an escrow company, which he said has been trying to return it to FTX. He said Lightcone never had any of it (https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php). A commenter in the EA Forum thread notes it is disputed whether FTX money paid for the Inn (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties).

4. Who bought it. The buyer was Lightcone, not CFAR alone. My recollection, which these sources do not confirm, is that other lenders and donors mainly financed the purchase.

The claim therefore presents as settled fact something that is contested and imprecise. It overstates the link between FTX money and the purchase, misnames the recipient, and gets the timing wrong.

## Research findings (background — not a source)
The claim is misleading. It says the property (Lighthaven, the former Rose Garden Inn in Berkeley) was originally bought with money wired from FTX to CFAR as FTX was collapsing. The evidence doesn't support that.

What the evidence shows:

The same complaint calls these a loan that was never repaid, and says a 'material portion' of other transfers to CFAR was used for the purchase and renovation. These are allegations, not findings. https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties
- The deposits were wired in July and August 2022. The sale closed around November 4, 2022, which is about when FTX collapsed. They were not wired during the collapse.
- The deposits went to a title/escrow company, not to CFAR. Lightcone's Oliver Habryka says no FTX funds were used to buy Lighthaven. He says the escrow company was trying to return the $1M, and he posted a 2022 escrow document saying the $1M would go back to an FTX-linked company. https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php and https://protos.com/ftx-chasing-5m-spent-on-right-wing-conference-venue/

The claim therefore states a contested allegation as settled fact. It overstates FTX's role in funding the purchase and is imprecise about when and where the money went.

For example, whether or not Richard Hanania uses prediction markets, I want him nowhere near EA or EA-funded groups/events. For why, [see this](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hanania#Writing_as_%22Richard_Hoste%22_\(2008%E2%80%93early_2010s\)).

## Cause Areas

Between humans and other animals, there are trillions of individuals in the world to help. A key idea in effective altruism is prioritizing important and neglected problems where there seems to be a strong potential for real change.

This leads people and organizations across the movement to focus on different areas of impact where they think they can do the most good.

[Global Health & Development Every year, millions of people die of illnesses that could be easily treated or prevented. ## Research findings (background — not a source)
The claim is broadly accurate but oversimplified. Effective Altruism (EA) has no single binding 'creed'. It is a philosophy and community built on using evidence and reason to do the most good. 'Earning to give' is one recognized career path within EA. It was popularized by 80,000 Hours around 2011–2013, and William MacAskill and Peter Singer have both promoted it. It is not a universal prescription. From about 2015–2023, 80,000 Hours moved away from recommending earning to give as the default for most people. Instead it emphasized direct work in high-impact fields such as AI safety, biosecurity and policy. It said that only some people, whose skills fit, should pursue high-earning careers. It also said people should not take harmful jobs. EA's core principle is maximizing impact, not maximizing earnings. The article's wording presents earning more as an EA creed for members generally, and that overstates how central or mandatory it is. I did not run a live search, so I have no source URL to cite. Relevant sources are 80,000 Hours' earning-to-give article, https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/, and the Centre for Effective Altruism's page, https://www.effectivealtruism.org/.

cascade.findings: The claim is broadly accurate as a description of the Effective Altruism concept of 'earning to give'. 80,000 Hours, the EA-affiliated career advisory org, defines earning to give as taking a job where you earn more money than you would have otherwise and donate much of the extra to fund others doing effective work, typically donating 20-50% to highly effective organisations, with finance and tech/software and founding companies given as typical routes https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/ . Wikipedia similarly defines earning to give as deliberately pursuing a high-earning career for the purpose of donating a significant portion of earned income https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_altruism . Nuance: it is not a universal creed/requirement for all EAs. 80,000 Hours explicitly says 'many people think it's our top recommendation for the majority of people. But it's not. Whether you should choose earning to give depends on your situation' and lists direct work, flexibility, personal fit considerations https://80000hours.org/articles/earning-to-give/ . EA's stated core is impartial maximising of good, cause prioritization and cost-effectiveness, with varied career paths including direct research, policy and nonprofit work https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_altruism . The article's phrasing 'by creed, says you should' therefore overstates universality, but as an explanation for why some EAs go into finance to give more, it captures a real, promoted doctrine.

cascade.findings: Claim overstates a real EA idea as a universal creed prescription. 'Earning to give' is real: it 'involves deliberately pursuing a high-earning career for the purpose of donating a significant portion of earned income, typically because of a desire to do effective altruism' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earning_to_give — jobs in finance, particularly quantitative trading, are popular for those pursuing it https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earning_to_give. That same EA source says: 'One path within effective altruism is called earning to give, whereby someone seeks out a high-paying career in order to donate a substantial portion' https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/misconceptions-and-concerns-about-effective-altruism-and-charity-evaluation, and 'Media coverage often mistakenly equates effective altruism entirely with this one path even though only some people within the community take this route' https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/misconceptions-and-concerns-about-effective-altruism-and-charity-evaluation, noting '80,000 Hours... believes earning to give is only right for a small proportion of people' https://www.givingwhatwecan.org/misconceptions-and-concerns-about-effective-altruism-and-charity-evaluation. So finance-to-donate happens, but presenting it as what EA 'by creed says you should' do is a misleading generalization.

cascade.findings:
The article interprets Yudkowsky's 'pivotal act' as terrorism anyone building AGI 'must do' to stop competition. Yudkowsky's own definition is narrower: 'We need to align the performance of some large task, a 'pivotal act' that prevents other people from building an unaligned AGI that destroys the world. While the number of actors with AGI is few or one, they must execute some "pivotal act", strong enough to flip the gameboard, using an AGI powerful enough to do that.' https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uMQ3cqWDPHhjtiesc/agi-ruin-a-list-of-lethalities

His stock example is '"burn all GPUs"' but he explicitly says 'This is not what I think you'd actually want to do' and 'I don't *actually* advocate doing that; it's just a mild overestimate for the rough power level of what you'd have to do, and the rough level of machine cognition required to do that, in order to prevent somebody else from destroying the world in six months or three years.' https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uMQ3cqWDPHhjtiesc/agi-ruin-a-list-of-lethalities

Summaries stress it is the first / whoever-builds-first actor using an aligned AGI to do it, not 'anyone making AGI' as a general human obligation: 'To avoid catastrophe, whoever builds AGI first will have to a) align it to some extent, and b) decide not to scale it up beyond the point where their alignment techniques fail, and c) do some pivotal act that prevents others from scaling it up to that level.' https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uMQ3cqWDPHhjtiesc/agi-ruin-a-list-of-lethalities and 'it may be necessary for the first lab that creates a sufficiently aligned AGI to perform a pivotal act to prevent the other labs from creating an unaligned AGI.' https://github.com/centresecuriteia/textbook/blob/main/docs/chapters/03/04.md

Motive is framed as preventing omnicide ('prevent Facebook AI Research from destroying the world six months later'), not commercial 'competition' https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uMQ3cqWDPHhjtiesc/agi-ruin-a-list-of-lethalities . Separately, in his 2023 Time op-ed Yudkowsky advocated state action under treaty — 'including an indefinite worldwide moratorium on large AI training runs' with participating countries willing to take military action, such as 'destroy[ing] a rogue datacenter by airstrike', to enforce such a moratorium https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliezer_Yudkowsky — i.e. government military/law-enforcement, not non-state 'terrorism' by AGI builders, and to be performed by/through AGI, not humans committing terrorist attacks.
