## Context
Current date (UTC): 2026-10-20T07:40:15.288Z

## Proposed community note
EA emerged from several communities, including GiveWell’s charity community, MIRI, the Future of Humanity Institute and LessWrong. Its core organization, the Centre for Effective Altruism, was founded by Oxford philosophers Toby Ord and William MacAskill.

## Note's cited sources (verify these)
### https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_altruism
# Effective altruism

**Effective altruism** (**EA**) is a 21st-century [philosophical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophical_movement "Philosophical movement") and [social movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_movement "Social movement") that advocates impartially calculating benefits and prioritizing causes to provide the greatest good. Proponents describe the movement as "using [evidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_evidence "Scientific evidence") and [reason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason "Reason") to figure out how to benefit others as much as possible, and taking action on that basis".[\[1\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2017-1)[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) People who pursue the goals of effective altruism, who are sometimes called _effective altruists_,[\[a\]](#cite_note-3) follow a variety of approaches proposed by the movement, such as donating to selected [charities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charities "Charities") and choosing careers, with the goal of maximising positive impact. The movement has spurred the creation of [research centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_centers "Research centers"), advisory organizations, and charities, which collectively have donated several hundred million dollars.[\[3\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAdamsCraryGruen2023xxii-4)

A defining feature of effective altruism is impartiality, specifically the global [equal consideration of interests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_consideration_of_interests "Equal consideration of interests") when choosing beneficiaries. Popular [cause priorities](#Cause_priorities) within effective altruism include [global health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_health "Global health") and [development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_development "Economic development"), [social](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_inequality "Social inequality") and [economic inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_inequality "Economic inequality"), [animal welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_welfare "Animal welfare"), and [risks to the survival or flourishing of humanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_catastrophic_risks "Global catastrophic risks") over the [long-term future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longtermism "Longtermism"). Only a small portion of all charities are affiliated with effective altruism, except in niche areas such as [farmed-animal welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_welfare#Farmed_animals "Animal welfare"), [AI safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_safety "AI safety"), and [biosecurity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biosecurity "Biosecurity").[\[4\]](#cite_note-5)

The movement developed during the 2000s, and the name _effective altruism_ was coined in 2011. Philosophers influential to the movement include [Peter Singer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer "Peter Singer"), [Toby Ord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Ord "Toby Ord"), and [William MacAskill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_MacAskill "William MacAskill"). Effective altruism is most popular within the [Anglosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglosphere "Anglosphere"), with concentrations at elite universities in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), as well as in and around the technology industry in the [San Francisco Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area").[\[5\]](#cite_note-6)

Some have argued that effective altruism focuses on incremental interventions instead of systemic or political interventions. The movement received mainstream attention and criticism with the [bankruptcy of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_FTX "Bankruptcy of FTX") in 2022 as founder [Sam Bankman-Fried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Bankman-Fried "Sam Bankman-Fried") was a major funder of effective altruism.[\[6\]](#cite_note-FTX_2021-7)[\[7\]](#cite_note-Howcroft_2023-8) Some women in the [San Francisco Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area") criticized what they described as a culture of sexual misconduct occurring among some participants in the movement. Proponents of the term [TESCREAL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TESCREAL "TESCREAL") argue that effective altruism is part of an overlapping bundle of movements.

[![Picture of Peter Singer](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/Peter_Singer_MIT_Veritas.jpg/250px-Peter_Singer_MIT_Veritas.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Peter_Singer_MIT_Veritas.jpg)

[![Picture of William MacAskill](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/William_MacAskill_Portrait_2015_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-William_MacAskill_Portrait_2015_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:William_MacAskill_Portrait_2015_\(cropped\).jpg)

Beginning in the latter half of the 2000s, several communities centered around altruist, [rationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationalist_community "Rationalist community"), and [futurological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futures_studies "Futures studies") concerns started to converge, such as:[\[8\]](#cite_note-Anthis_2022-9)

*   The evidence-based charity community centered around [GiveWell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GiveWell "GiveWell"),[\[9\]](#cite_note-10) including [Open Philanthropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Philanthropy "Open Philanthropy"), which originally came out of GiveWell Labs but then became independent.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Matthews_2015b-11)[\[11\]](#cite_note-12)
*   The community around pledging and career selection for effective giving, centered around the [Giving What We Can](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giving_What_We_Can "Giving What We Can") and [80,000 Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/80,000_Hours "80,000 Hours") nonprofits.[\[12\]](#cite_note-13)
*   The [Singularity Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singularity_Institute "Singularity Institute") (now [MIRI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_Intelligence_Research_Institute "Machine Intelligence Research Institute")) for studying the [safety of artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment "AI alignment"), the [Future of Humanity Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_of_Humanity_Institute "Future of Humanity Institute") studying topics such as [existential risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risk "Existential risk"), and the _[LessWrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LessWrong "LessWrong")_ discussion forum, which focuses on rationalism.[\[13\]](#cite_note-14)

In 2011, Giving What We Can and 80,000 Hours decided to incorporate into an [umbrella organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umbrella_organization "Umbrella organization") and held a vote for their new name; the "Centre for Effective Altruism" was selected.[\[14\]](#cite_note-15)[\[15\]](#cite_note-Singer_2015-16) The [Effective Altruism Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_Altruism_Global "Effective Altruism Global") conference has been held since 2013. As the movement formed, it attracted individuals who were not part of a specific community, but who had been following the Australian moral philosopher [Peter Singer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer "Peter Singer")'s work on [applied ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_ethics "Applied ethics"), particularly "[Famine, Affluence, and Morality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine,_Affluence,_and_Morality "Famine, Affluence, and Morality")" (1972), _[Animal Liberation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_Liberation_\(book\) "Animal Liberation (book)")_ (1975), and _[The Life You Can Save](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Life_You_Can_Save "The Life You Can Save")_ (2009).[\[8\]](#cite_note-Anthis_2022-9)[\[16\]](#cite_note-Lichtenberg_2015-17) Singer himself used the term in 2013, in a [TED talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TED_talk "TED talk") titled "The Why and How of Effective Altruism".[\[17\]](#cite_note-18)

### Notable philanthropists

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Notable philanthropists")\]

An estimated $416 million was donated to effective charities identified by the movement in 2019,[\[18\]](#cite_note-19) representing a 37% annual growth rate since 2015.[\[19\]](#cite_note-20) Two of the largest donors in the effective altruism community, [Dustin Moskovitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dustin_Moskovitz "Dustin Moskovitz"), who had become wealthy through co-founding [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook"), and his wife [Cari Tuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cari_Tuna "Cari Tuna"), hope to donate most of their net worth of over $11 billion for effective altruist causes through the private foundation [Good Ventures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Ventures "Good Ventures") and are major funders of [Open Philanthropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Philanthropy "Open Philanthropy").[\[10\]](#cite_note-Matthews_2015b-11) Others influenced by effective altruism include Sam Bankman-Fried,[\[20\]](#cite_note-21) and professional poker players [Dan Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Smith_\(poker_player\) "Dan Smith (poker player)")[\[21\]](#cite_note-Pincus-Roth_2020-22) and [Liv Boeree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liv_Boeree "Liv Boeree").[\[21\]](#cite_note-Pincus-Roth_2020-22) [Jaan Tallinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaan_Tallinn "Jaan Tallinn"), the Estonian billionaire founder of [Skype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skype "Skype"), is known for donating to some effective altruist causes.[\[22\]](#cite_note-Matthews_2015a-23) Sam Bankman-Fried launched a philanthropic organization called the FTX Foundation in February 2021,[\[6\]](#cite_note-FTX_2021-7) and it made contributions to a number of effective altruist organizations, but it was shut down in November 2022 when [FTX collapsed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTX_collapsed "FTX collapsed").[\[7\]](#cite_note-Howcroft_2023-8) Actor [Joseph Gordon-Levitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Gordon-Levitt "Joseph Gordon-Levitt") has publicly stated he would like to bring the ideas of effective altruism to a broader audience.[\[23\]](#cite_note-Lewis-Kraus_2022b-24) Musician [José Gonzáles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_González_\(singer\) "José González (singer)") has been inspired by the effective altruist philosophy to donate 10% of his income since 2017, when he signed the [Giving What We Can](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giving_What_We_Can "Giving What We Can") pledge.[\[24\]](#cite_note-25)[\[25\]](#cite_note-26) [Elon Musk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_Musk "Elon Musk") spoke at an effective altruism conference in 2015.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Kulish_2022-27) He described MacAskill's 2022 book _[What We Owe the Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_We_Owe_the_Future "What We Owe the Future")_ as "a close match for my philosophy", but has not officially joined the movement.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Kulish_2022-27) An article in _[The Chronicle of Philanthropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Chronicle_of_Philanthropy "The Chronicle of Philanthropy")_ argued that the record of Musk's substantive alignment with effective altruism was "choppy",[\[27\]](#cite_note-28) and [Bloomberg News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_News "Bloomberg News") noted that his 2021 charitable contributions showed "few obvious signs that effective altruism ... impacted Musk's giving."[\[28\]](#cite_note-29)

### Notable publications and media

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Notable publications and media")\]

A number of books and articles related to effective altruism have been published that have codified, criticized, and brought more attention to the movement. In 2015, philosopher [Peter Singer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Singer "Peter Singer") published _[The Most Good You Can Do: How Effective Altruism Is Changing Ideas About Living Ethically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Most_Good_You_Can_Do:_How_Effective_Altruism_Is_Changing_Ideas_About_Living_Ethically "The Most Good You Can Do: How Effective Altruism Is Changing Ideas About Living Ethically")_.[\[29\]](#cite_note-Kristof_2015-30) The same year, the Scottish philosopher and ethicist [William MacAskill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_MacAskill "William MacAskill") published _[Doing Good Better: How Effective Altruism Can Help You Make a Difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doing_Good_Better "Doing Good Better")_.[\[30\]](#cite_note-31)[\[31\]](#cite_note-Thompson_2015-32) B.V.E. Hyde describes these two books as "the bibles of effective altruism".[\[32\]](#cite_note-Hyde_2025-33) In 2018, American news website _[Vox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vox_\(website\) "Vox (website)")_ launched its _Future Perfect_ section, led by journalist [Dylan Matthews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylan_Matthews "Dylan Matthews"), which publishes articles and podcasts on "finding the best ways to do good".[\[33\]](#cite_note-34)[\[34\]](#cite_note-35) In 2019, [Oxford University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University_Press "Oxford University Press") published the volume _Effective Altruism: Philosophical Issues_, edited by [Hilary Greaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilary_Greaves "Hilary Greaves") and Theron Pummer.[\[35\]](#cite_note-36) More recent books have emphasized concerns for future generations. In 2020, the Australian moral philosopher [Toby Ord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Ord "Toby Ord") published _[The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Precipice:_Existential_Risk_and_the_Future_of_Humanity "The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity")_,[\[36\]](#cite_note-37) while MacAskill published _[What We Owe the Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_We_Owe_the_Future "What We Owe the Future")_ in 2022.[\[37\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2022b-38) In 2023, Oxford University Press published the volume _The Good it Promises, The Harm it Does: Critical Essays on Effective Altruism_, edited by [Carol J. Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_J._Adams "Carol J. Adams"), [Alice Crary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Crary "Alice Crary"), and [Lori Gruen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lori_Gruen "Lori Gruen").[\[38\]](#cite_note-39)[\[39\]](#cite_note-Pettigrew_2023-40)

Effective altruists focus on the many philosophical questions related to the most effective ways to benefit others.[\[40\]](#cite_note-Pummer_2020-41)[\[41\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2019-42) Such philosophical questions shift the starting point of reasoning from "what to do" to "why" and "how".[\[42\]](#cite_note-Crouch_2013-43) There is not a consensus on the answers, and there are also differences between effective altruists who believe that they should do the most good they possibly can with all of their resources[\[b\]](#cite_note-44) and those who only try do the most good they can within a defined budget.[\[41\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2019-42): 15 

According to MacAskill, the view of effective altruism as doing the most good one can within a defined budget can be compatible with a wide variety of views on [morality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morality "Morality") and [meta-ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta-ethics "Meta-ethics"), as well as traditional religious teachings on altruism such as in [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity").[\[1\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2017-1)[\[40\]](#cite_note-Pummer_2020-41) Effective altruism can also be in tension with religion where religion emphasizes spending resources on worship and evangelism instead of causes that do the most good.[\[1\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2017-1) Other than Peter Singer and MacAskill, philosophers associated with effective altruism include [Nick Bostrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Bostrom "Nick Bostrom"),[\[22\]](#cite_note-Matthews_2015a-23) [Toby Ord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Ord "Toby Ord"),[\[43\]](#cite_note-45) [Hilary Greaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilary_Greaves "Hilary Greaves"),[\[44\]](#cite_note-46) and [Derek Parfit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Parfit "Derek Parfit").[\[45\]](#cite_note-47) Economist [Yew-Kwang Ng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yew-Kwang_Ng "Yew-Kwang Ng") conducted similar research in [welfare economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_economics "Welfare economics") and [moral philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_philosophy "Moral philosophy").[\[46\]](#cite_note-48)

The Centre for Effective Altruism lists the following four principles that unite effective altruism: prioritization, impartial altruism, open truthseeking, and a collaborative spirit.[\[47\]](#cite_note-Centre_for_Effective_Altruism-49) To support people's ability to act altruistically on the basis of impartial reasoning, the effective altruism movement promotes values and actions such as a collaborative spirit, honesty, transparency, and publicly pledging to donate a certain percentage of income or other resources.[\[1\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2017-1): 2 

Effective altruism aims to emphasize impartial reasoning in that everyone's [well-being](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-being "Well-being") counts equally.[\[48\]](#cite_note-50) Singer, in his 1972 essay "[Famine, Affluence, and Morality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine,_Affluence,_and_Morality "Famine, Affluence, and Morality")",[\[16\]](#cite_note-Lichtenberg_2015-17) wrote:

> It makes no moral difference whether the person I can help is a neighbor's child ten yards away from me or a Bengali whose name I shall never know, ten thousand miles away ... The moral point of view requires us to look beyond the interests of our own society.[\[49\]](#cite_note-Singer_1972-51): 231–232 

Impartiality combined with seeking to do the most good leads to prioritizing benefits to those who are in a worse state, because anyone who happens to be worse off will benefit more from an improvement in their state, all other things being equal.[\[40\]](#cite_note-Pummer_2020-41)[\[47\]](#cite_note-Centre_for_Effective_Altruism-49)

#### Scope of moral consideration

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Scope of moral consideration")\]

One issue related to moral impartiality is the question of which beings are deserving of moral consideration. Some effective altruists consider the well-being of non-human animals in addition to humans, and advocate for animal welfare issues such as ending [factory farming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factory_farming "Factory farming").[\[50\]](#cite_note-52) Those who subscribe to [longtermism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longtermism "Longtermism") include [future generations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_generations "Future generations") as possible beneficiaries and try to improve the moral value of the long-term future, for example by reducing [existential risks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risks "Existential risks").[\[15\]](#cite_note-Singer_2015-16): 165–178 [\[51\]](#cite_note-53)

#### Criticism of impartiality

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Criticism of impartiality")\]

The [drowning child analogy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drowning_child_analogy "Drowning child analogy") in Singer's essay provoked philosophical debate. In response to a version of Singer's drowning child analogy,[\[52\]](#cite_note-54) philosopher [Kwame Anthony Appiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Anthony_Appiah "Kwame Anthony Appiah") in 2006 asked whether the most effective action of a man in an expensive suit, confronted with a drowning child, would not be to save the child and ruin his suit—but rather, sell the suit and donate the proceeds to charity.[\[53\]](#cite_note-Appiah_2006-55)[\[54\]](#cite_note-56) Appiah believed that he "should save the drowning child and ruin my suit".[\[53\]](#cite_note-Appiah_2006-55) In a 2015 debate, when presented with a similar scenario of either saving a child from a burning building or saving a [Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picasso "Picasso") painting to sell and donate the proceeds to charity, MacAskill responded that the effective altruist should save and sell the Picasso.[\[55\]](#cite_note-57) Psychologist Alan Jern called MacAskill's choice "unnatural, even distasteful, to many people", although Jern concluded that effective altruism raises questions "worth asking".[\[56\]](#cite_note-58) MacAskill later endorsed a "qualified definition of effective altruism" in which effective altruists try to do the most good "without violating constraints" such as any obligations that someone might have to help those nearby.[\[57\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2019a-59)

William Schambra has criticized the impartial logic of effective altruism, arguing that benevolence arising from [reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocity_\(social_psychology\) "Reciprocity (social psychology)") and face-to-face interactions is stronger and more prevalent than charity based on impartial, detached altruism.[\[58\]](#cite_note-Schambra_2014-60) Such community-based charitable giving, he wrote, is foundational to [civil society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_society "Civil society") and, in turn, [democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy "Democracy").[\[58\]](#cite_note-Schambra_2014-60) [Larissa MacFarquhar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larissa_MacFarquhar "Larissa MacFarquhar") said that people have diverse moral emotions, and she suggested that some effective altruists are not unemotional and detached but feel as much empathy for distant strangers as for people nearby.[\[59\]](#cite_note-61) Richard Pettigrew concurred that many effective altruists "feel more profound dismay at the suffering of people unknown to them than many people feel", and he argued that impartiality in EA need not be dispassionate and "is not obviously in tension with much in [care ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Care_ethics "Care ethics")" as some philosophers have argued.[\[39\]](#cite_note-Pettigrew_2023-40) [Ross Douthat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Douthat "Ross Douthat") of _The New York Times_ criticized the movement's "'telescopic philanthropy' aimed at distant populations" and envisioned "effective altruists sitting around in a San Francisco skyscraper calculating how to relieve suffering halfway around the world while the city decays beneath them", while he also praised the movement for providing "useful rebukes to the solipsism and anti-human pessimism that haunts the developed world today".[\[60\]](#cite_note-62)

### Cause prioritization

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Cause prioritization")\]

A key component of effective altruism is "cause prioritization". Cause prioritization is based on the principle of cause _neutrality_, the idea that resources should be distributed to causes based on what will do the most good, irrespective of the identity of the beneficiary and the way in which they are helped.[\[40\]](#cite_note-Pummer_2020-41) By contrast, many non-profits emphasize effectiveness and evidence with respect to a single cause such as education or climate change.[\[58\]](#cite_note-Schambra_2014-60)

One tool that EA-based organizations may use to prioritize cause areas is the _importance, tractability, and neglectedness_ framework. Importance is the amount of value that would be created if a problem were solved, tractability is the fraction of a problem that would be solved if additional resources were devoted to it, and neglectedness is the quantity of resources already committed to a cause.[\[23\]](#cite_note-Lewis-Kraus_2022b-24)

The information required for cause prioritization may involve [data analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_analysis "Data analysis"), comparing possible outcomes with what would have happened under other conditions ([counterfactual reasoning](#Counterfactual_reasoning)), and identifying [uncertainty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty "Uncertainty").[\[40\]](#cite_note-Pummer_2020-41)[\[61\]](#cite_note-63) The difficulty of these tasks has led to the creation of organizations that specialize in researching the relative prioritization of causes.[\[40\]](#cite_note-Pummer_2020-41)

#### Criticism of cause prioritization

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Criticism of cause prioritization")\]

This practice of "weighing causes and beneficiaries against one another" was criticized by Ken Berger and Robert Penna of [Charity Navigator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charity_Navigator "Charity Navigator") for being "moralistic, in the worst sense of the word" and "elitist".[\[62\]](#cite_note-64) William MacAskill responded to Berger and Penna, defending the rationale for comparing one beneficiary's interests against another and concluding that such comparison is difficult and sometimes impossible but often necessary.[\[63\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2013-65) MacAskill argued that the more pernicious form of elitism was that of donating to art galleries (and like institutions) instead of charity.[\[63\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2013-65) Ian David Moss suggested that the criticism of cause prioritization could be resolved by what he called "domain-specific effective altruism", which would encourage "that principles of effective altruism be followed within an area of philanthropic focus, such as a specific cause or geography" and could resolve the conflict between local and global perspectives for some donors.[\[64\]](#cite_note-66)

Some charities are considered to be far more effective than others, as charities may spend different amounts of money to achieve the same goal, and some charities may not achieve the goal at all.[\[65\]](#cite_note-67) Effective altruists seek to identify interventions that are highly cost-effective in [expectation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value "Expected value"). Many interventions have [uncertain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncertainty "Uncertainty") benefits, and the expected value of one intervention can be higher than that of another if its benefits are larger, even if it has a smaller chance of succeeding.[\[31\]](#cite_note-Thompson_2015-32) One metric effective altruists use to choose between health interventions is the estimated number of [quality-adjusted life years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality-adjusted_life_year "Quality-adjusted life year") (QALY) added per dollar.[\[23\]](#cite_note-Lewis-Kraus_2022b-24)

Some effective altruist organizations prefer [randomized controlled trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randomized_controlled_trial "Randomized controlled trial") as a primary form of evidence,[\[31\]](#cite_note-Thompson_2015-32)[\[66\]](#cite_note-Skelton_2016-68) as they are commonly considered the highest level of evidence in healthcare research.[\[67\]](#cite_note-69) Others have argued that requiring this stringent level of evidence unnecessarily narrows the focus to issues where the evidence can be developed.[\[68\]](#cite_note-Rubenstein_2016-70) [Kelsey Piper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelsey_Piper "Kelsey Piper") argues that uncertainty is not a good reason for effective altruists to avoid acting on their best understanding of the world, because most interventions have mixed evidence regarding their effectiveness.[\[69\]](#cite_note-Piper_2022-71)

Pascal-Emmanuel Gobry and others have warned about the "[measurement problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McNamara_fallacy "McNamara fallacy")",[\[68\]](#cite_note-Rubenstein_2016-70)[\[70\]](#cite_note-Gobry_2015-72) with issues such as medical research or government reform worked on "one grinding step at a time", and results being hard to measure with controlled experiments. Gobry also argues that such interventions risk being undervalued by the effective altruism movement.[\[70\]](#cite_note-Gobry_2015-72) As effective altruism emphasizes a data-centric approach, critics say principles which do not lend themselves to quantification—justice, fairness, equality—get left in the sidelines.[\[23\]](#cite_note-Lewis-Kraus_2022b-24)[\[31\]](#cite_note-Thompson_2015-32)

### Counterfactual reasoning

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Counterfactual reasoning")\]

[Counterfactual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterfactual_conditional "Counterfactual conditional") reasoning involves considering the possible outcomes of alternative choices. It has been employed by effective altruists in a number of contexts, including career choice. Many people assume that the best way to help others is through direct methods, such as working for a charity or providing social services.[\[71\]](#cite_note-73) However, since there is a high supply of candidates for such positions, it makes sense to compare the amount of good one candidate does to how much good the next-best candidate would do. According to this reasoning, the marginal impact of a career is likely to be smaller than the gross impact.[\[72\]](#cite_note-74)

### Differences from utilitarianism

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Differences from utilitarianism")\]

MacAskill has argued that unlike [utilitarianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utilitarianism "Utilitarianism"), EA does not claim that people should always maximize the good regardless of the means or that well-being is the only source of [intrinsic value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrinsic_value_\(ethics\) "Intrinsic value (ethics)").[\[57\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2019a-59) Toby Ord has described utilitarians as "number-crunching", compared with most effective altruists whom he called "guided by conventional wisdom tempered by an eye to the numbers".[\[73\]](#cite_note-75) Other philosophers have argued that EA still retains some core ethical commitments that are essential and distinctive to utilitarianism, such as the principle of impartiality, [welfarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfarism "Welfarism") and good-maximization.[\[74\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAdamsCraryGruen2023xxvi-76)

MacAskill has argued that one should not be absolutely certain about which ethical view is correct, and that "when we are morally uncertain, we should act in a way that serves as a best compromise between different moral views".[\[37\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2022b-38) He also wrote that even from a purely [consequentialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequentialist "Consequentialist") perspective, "naive calculations that justify some harmful action because it has good consequences are, in practice, almost never correct".[\[37\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2022b-38)

### Differences from effective accelerationism

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Differences from effective accelerationism")\]

[Effective accelerationism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_accelerationism "Effective accelerationism") (abbreviated e/acc) is influenced by ideas of [accelerationism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accelerationism "Accelerationism"). Its proponents advocate unrestricted technological progress in the hope that [artificial general intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_general_intelligence "Artificial general intelligence") will solve major challenges and maximize overall good, arguing that deceleration and stagnation of technology is a greater risk than any posed by AI. Effective altruists are generally more cautious about AI, based on their belief that going too fast could increase [existential risks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risk_from_artificial_intelligence "Existential risk from artificial intelligence").[\[75\]](#cite_note-77)

The principles and goals of effective altruism are wide enough to support furthering any cause that allows people to do the most good, while taking into account cause neutrality.[\[42\]](#cite_note-Crouch_2013-43) B.V.E. Hyde distinguishes between the effective altruist movement (EAM) and effective altruist theory (EAT) which, he argues, have very different focusses.[\[32\]](#cite_note-Hyde_2025-33) Many people in the effective altruism movement have prioritized global health and development, animal welfare, and mitigating risks that threaten the future of humanity.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Matthews_2015b-11)[\[66\]](#cite_note-Skelton_2016-68)

### Global health and development

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Global health and development")\]

The alleviation of [global poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_poverty "Global poverty") and [neglected tropical diseases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neglected_tropical_diseases "Neglected tropical diseases") has been a focus of some of the earliest and most prominent organizations associated with effective altruism. Charity evaluator GiveWell was founded by [Holden Karnofsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holden_Karnofsky "Holden Karnofsky") and [Elie Hassenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elie_Hassenfeld "Elie Hassenfeld") in 2007 to address poverty,[\[76\]](#cite_note-78) where they believe additional donations to be the most impactful.[\[77\]](#cite_note-79) GiveWell's leading recommendations include: [malaria prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaria_prevention "Malaria prevention") charities [Against Malaria Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Against_Malaria_Foundation "Against Malaria Foundation") and [Malaria Consortium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaria_Consortium "Malaria Consortium"), [deworming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deworming "Deworming") charities [Schistosomiasis Control Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schistosomiasis_Control_Initiative "Schistosomiasis Control Initiative") and [Deworm the World Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deworm_the_World_Initiative "Deworm the World Initiative"), and [GiveDirectly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GiveDirectly "GiveDirectly") for direct cash transfers to beneficiaries.[\[78\]](#cite_note-80)[\[79\]](#cite_note-81) The organization The Life You Can Save, which originated from Singer's book _[The Life You Can Save](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Life_You_Can_Save "The Life You Can Save")_,[\[80\]](#cite_note-82) works to alleviate global poverty by promoting evidence-backed charities, conducting philanthropy education, and changing the culture of giving in affluent countries.[\[81\]](#cite_note-83)

Improving animal welfare has been a focus of many effective altruists.[\[82\]](#cite_note-84) Singer and [Animal Charity Evaluators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_Charity_Evaluators "Animal Charity Evaluators") (ACE) have argued that effective altruists should prioritize changes to factory farming over pet welfare.[\[29\]](#cite_note-Kristof_2015-30) Over 80 billion land animals are [slaughtered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_slaughter "Animal slaughter") and between 1 and 2.7 trillion individual fish are killed each year for human consumption.[\[83\]](#cite_note-85) A number of non-profit organizations have been established that adopt an effective altruist approach toward animal welfare. ACE evaluates animal charities based on their cost-effectiveness and transparency, particularly those tackling factory farming.[\[15\]](#cite_note-Singer_2015-16): 139 [\[84\]](#cite_note-86) [Faunalytics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faunalytics "Faunalytics") focuses on animal welfare research.[\[85\]](#cite_note-87) Other animal initiatives affiliated with effective altruism include [Animal Ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_Ethics_\(organization\) "Animal Ethics (organization)")' and [Wild Animal Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_Animal_Initiative "Wild Animal Initiative")'s work on [wild animal suffering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_animal_suffering "Wild animal suffering"),[\[86\]](#cite_note-88)[\[87\]](#cite_note-89) addressing farm animal suffering with [cultured meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultured_meat "Cultured meat"),[\[88\]](#cite_note-90) and increasing concern for all kinds of animals.[\[89\]](#cite_note-Torrella_2021-91)[\[90\]](#cite_note-92) The [Sentience Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentience_Institute "Sentience Institute") is a [think tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Think_tank "Think tank") founded to [expand the moral circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_circle_expansion "Moral circle expansion") to other [sentient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentience "Sentience") beings.[\[91\]](#cite_note-93)

### Long-term future and global catastrophic risks

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Long-term future and global catastrophic risks")\]

The ethical stance of [longtermism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longtermism "Longtermism"), emphasizing the importance of positively influencing the long-term future, developed closely in relation to effective altruism.[\[92\]](#cite_note-94)[\[93\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2022a-95) Longtermism argues that "distance in time is like distance in space", suggesting that the welfare of future individuals matters as much as the welfare of currently existing individuals. Given the potentially extremely high number of individuals that could exist in the future, longtermists seek to decrease the probability that an existential catastrophe irreversibly ruins it.[\[94\]](#cite_note-96) Toby Ord has stated that "the people of the future may be even more powerless to protect themselves from the risks we impose than the dispossessed of our own time".[\[95\]](#cite_note-97): 8 

[Existential risks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risk "Existential risk"), such as dangers associated with [biotechnology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotechnology "Biotechnology") and [advanced artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risk_from_advanced_artificial_intelligence "Existential risk from advanced artificial intelligence"), are often highlighted and the subject of active research.[\[93\]](#cite_note-MacAskill_2022a-95) Existential risks have such huge impacts that achieving a very small change in such a risk—say a 0.0001-percent reduction—"might be worth more than saving a billion people today", reported Gideon Lewis-Kraus in 2022, but he added that nobody in the EA community openly endorses such an extreme conclusion.[\[23\]](#cite_note-Lewis-Kraus_2022b-24)

Organizations devoted to working on research and advocacy for improving the long-term future, and connected to the effective altruism community, include the [Centre for the Study of Existential Risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_the_Study_of_Existential_Risk "Centre for the Study of Existential Risk") at the University of Cambridge, the [Future of Life Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_of_Life_Institute "Future of Life Institute"), and the now-defunct [Future of Humanity Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_of_Humanity_Institute "Future of Humanity Institute") at the University of Oxford.[\[96\]](#cite_note-98) In addition, the [Machine Intelligence Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_Intelligence_Research_Institute "Machine Intelligence Research Institute") is focused on the more narrow mission of [managing advanced artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_risk_from_artificial_general_intelligence#Mitigation "Existential risk from artificial general intelligence").[\[97\]](#cite_note-99)

Some effective altruists focus on reducing risks of astronomical suffering (s-risks). S-risks are a particularly severe type of existential risk due to their potential scope and severity, surpassing even human extinction in negative impact. Efforts to mitigate these risks include research and advocacy by organizations like the Center on Long-Term Risk, which explores strategies to avoid large-scale suffering. S-risks could arise from a long-term neglect for the welfare of some types of sentient beings. Another suggested scenario involves repressive totalitarian regimes that would become irreversibly stable due to advanced technology.[\[98\]](#cite_note-100)[\[99\]](#cite_note-101)

Effective altruists pursue different approaches to doing good, such as donating to effective charitable organizations, using their career to make more money for donations or directly contributing their labor, and starting new non-profit or for-profit ventures.

Many effective altruists engage in charitable [donation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donation "Donation"). Some believe it is a moral duty to alleviate [suffering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffering "Suffering") through donations if other possible uses of those funds do not offer comparable benefits to oneself.[\[49\]](#cite_note-Singer_1972-51) Some lead a [frugal lifestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frugality "Frugality") in order to donate more.[\[100\]](#cite_note-102) Giving What We Can (GWWC) is an organization whose members pledge to donate at least 10% of their future income to the causes that they believe are the most effective. GWWC was founded in 2009 by Toby Ord, who lives on £18,000 ($27,000) per year and donates the balance of his income.[\[101\]](#cite_note-103) In 2020, Ord said that people had donated over $100 million to date through the GWWC pledge.[\[102\]](#cite_note-104) [Founders Pledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founders_Pledge "Founders Pledge") is a similar initiative, founded out of the non-profit Founders Forum for Good, whereby entrepreneurs make a legally binding commitment to donate a percentage of their personal proceeds to charity in the event that they sell their business.[\[103\]](#cite_note-105) As of April 2024, nearly 1,900 entrepreneurs had pledged around $10 billion and nearly $1.1 billion had been donated.[\[104\]](#cite_note-106)

EA has been used to argue that humans should [donate organs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_donation "Organ donation"), whilst alive or after death, and some effective altruists do.[\[105\]](#cite_note-107)

Effective altruists often consider using their career to do good,[\[106\]](#cite_note-108) both by direct service and indirectly through their consumption, investment, and donation decisions.[\[107\]](#cite_note-109) 80,000 Hours is an organization that conducts research and gives advice on which careers have the largest positive impact.[\[108\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews2018a-110)[\[109\]](#cite_note-111)

[Earning to give](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earning_to_give "Earning to give") involves deliberately pursuing a high-earning career for the purpose of donating a significant portion of earned income, typically because of a desire to do effective altruism. Advocates of earning to give contend that maximizing the amount one can donate to charity is an important consideration for individuals when deciding what career to pursue.[\[110\]](#cite_note-Earning_to_give_kristof-112)

### Open-source contributions and open collaboration

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Open-source contributions and open collaboration")\]

[Open-source software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software") development has been used by organizations associated with effective altruism. Effective altruism events have included collaborative [hackathons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackathon "Hackathon"); EAGxBerkeley 2022, for example, included a post-conference hackathon.[\[111\]](#cite_note-113)

Open-source software has been studied as the voluntary provision of a [public good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_good_\(economics\) "Public good (economics)"), since contributors invest effort in software that can subsequently be used and further developed by others.[\[112\]](#cite_note-114) Research examining the motivations of open-source contributors has also found altruism to be an important motivation for participation.[\[113\]](#cite_note-115)

### Founding effective organizations

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Founding effective organizations")\]

Some effective altruists start non-profit or for-profit organizations to implement [cost-effective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost-effective "Cost-effective") ways of doing good. On the non-profit side, for example, [Michael Kremer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Kremer "Michael Kremer") and [Rachel Glennerster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Glennerster "Rachel Glennerster") conducted [randomized controlled trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randomized_controlled_trial "Randomized controlled trial") in Kenya to find out the best way to improve students' test scores. They tried new textbooks and flip charts, as well as smaller class sizes, but found that the only intervention that raised school attendance was treating intestinal worms in children. Based on their findings, they started the [Deworm the World Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deworm_the_World_Initiative "Deworm the World Initiative").[\[31\]](#cite_note-Thompson_2015-32) From 2013 to August 2022, GiveWell designated Deworm the World (now run by nonprofit [Evidence Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evidence_Action "Evidence Action")) as a top charity based on their assessment that [mass deworming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_deworming "Mass deworming") is "generally highly cost-effective";[\[114\]](#cite_note-116) however, there is substantial uncertainty about the benefits of mass deworming programs, with some studies finding long-term effects and others not.[\[69\]](#cite_note-Piper_2022-71) The Happier Lives Institute conducts research on the effectiveness of [cognitive behavioral therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_behavioral_therapy "Cognitive behavioral therapy") (CBT) in developing countries;[\[115\]](#cite_note-117) Canopie develops an app that provides cognitive behavioural therapy to women who are expecting or postpartum;[\[116\]](#cite_note-118) Giving Green analyzes and ranks climate interventions for effectiveness;[\[117\]](#cite_note-119) the Fish Welfare Initiative works on improving animal welfare in fishing and aquaculture;[\[89\]](#cite_note-Torrella_2021-91) and the [Lead Exposure Elimination Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_Exposure_Elimination_Project "Lead Exposure Elimination Project") works on reducing [lead poisoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_poisoning "Lead poisoning") in developing countries.[\[118\]](#cite_note-120)

## Psychological research

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Psychological research")\]

Researchers in [psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology "Psychology") and related fields have identified psychological barriers to effective altruism that can cause people to choose other options when they engage in altruistic activities such as charitable giving.[\[119\]](#cite_note-121)

## Other criticism and controversies

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Other criticism and controversies")\]

Although the movement's original leaders were associated with frugal lifestyles, the arrival of big donors, including Bankman-Fried, led to more spending and opulence, which seemed incongruous with the movement's espoused values.[\[120\]](#cite_note-Lewis-Kraus_2022a-122)[\[121\]](#cite_note-Wenar_2024-123) In 2022, Effective Ventures Foundation purchased the estate of [Wytham Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wytham_Abbey "Wytham Abbey") for the purpose of running workshops,[\[23\]](#cite_note-Lewis-Kraus_2022b-24) but put it up for sale in 2024.[\[122\]](#cite_note-124)

### Incremental versus systemic change

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Incremental versus systemic change")\]

While much of the initial focus of effective altruism was on direct strategies such as health interventions and cash transfers, more [systematic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_fix "Structural fix") social, economic, and political reforms have also attracted attention.[\[123\]](#cite_note-125) Mathew Snow in _[Jacobin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobin_\(magazine\) "Jacobin (magazine)")_ wrote that effective altruism "implores individuals to use their money to procure necessities for those who desperately need them, but says nothing about the system that determines how those necessities are produced and distributed in the first place".[\[124\]](#cite_note-126) Philosopher [Amia Srinivasan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amia_Srinivasan "Amia Srinivasan") criticized William MacAskill's _[Doing Good Better](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doing_Good_Better "Doing Good Better")_ for a perceived lack of coverage of [global inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_inequality "Global inequality") and [oppression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppression "Oppression"), while noting that effective altruism is in principle open to whichever means of doing good is most effective, including political advocacy aimed at systemic change.[\[125\]](#cite_note-Srinivasan_2015-127) Srinivasan said, "Effective altruism has so far been a rather homogeneous movement of middle-class white men fighting poverty through largely conventional means, but it is at least in theory a broad church."[\[125\]](#cite_note-Srinivasan_2015-127) [Judith Lichtenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Lichtenberg "Judith Lichtenberg") in _[The New Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Republic "The New Republic")_ said that effective altruists "neglect the kind of structural and political change that is ultimately necessary".[\[126\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELichtenberg2015-128) An article in _[The Ecologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ecologist "The Ecologist")_ published in 2016 argued that effective altruism is an apolitical attempt to solve political problems, describing the concept as "pseudo-scientific".[\[127\]](#cite_note-129) The Ethiopian-American AI scientist [Timnit Gebru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timnit_Gebru "Timnit Gebru") has condemned effective altruists "for acting as though their concerns are above structural issues as racism and colonialism", as Gideon Lewis-Kraus summarized her views in 2022.[\[23\]](#cite_note-Lewis-Kraus_2022b-24)

Philosophers such as Susan Dwyer, Joshua Stein, and [Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olúfẹ́mi_O._Táíwò "Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò") have criticized effective altruism for furthering the disproportionate influence of wealthy individuals in domains that should be the responsibility of democratic governments and organizations.[\[128\]](#cite_note-130) Arguments have been made that movements focused on systemic or institutional change, for example [democratization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratization "Democratization"), are compatible with effective altruism.[\[129\]](#cite_note-131)[\[130\]](#cite_note-132)[\[131\]](#cite_note-133) Philosopher Elizabeth Ashford posits that people are obligated to both donate to effective aid charities and to [reform the structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_change "Structural change") that are responsible for poverty.[\[132\]](#cite_note-134) Open Philanthropy has given grants for progressive advocacy work in areas such as criminal justice,[\[10\]](#cite_note-Matthews_2015b-11)[\[133\]](#cite_note-135) economic stabilization,[\[10\]](#cite_note-Matthews_2015b-11) and housing reform,[\[134\]](#cite_note-136) despite pegging the success of political reform as being "highly uncertain".[\[10\]](#cite_note-Matthews_2015b-11)

[Sam Bankman-Fried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Bankman-Fried "Sam Bankman-Fried"), the eventual founder of the [cryptocurrency exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptocurrency_exchange "Cryptocurrency exchange") [FTX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTX_\(company\) "FTX (company)"), had a lunch with philosopher [William MacAskill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_MacAskill "William MacAskill") in 2012 while he was an undergraduate at MIT in which MacAskill encouraged him to go earn money and donate it, rather than volunteering his time for causes.[\[135\]](#cite_note-Tiku_2022-137)[\[26\]](#cite_note-Kulish_2022-27) Bankman-Fried went on to a career in investing and around 2019 became more publicly associated with the effective altruism movement,[\[136\]](#cite_note-138) announcing that his goal was to "donate as much as \[he\] can".[\[137\]](#cite_note-139) Bankman-Fried founded the FTX Future Fund, which brought on MacAskill as one of its advisers, and which made a $13.9 million grant to the [Centre for Effective Altruism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Effective_Altruism "Centre for Effective Altruism") where MacAskill holds a board role.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Kulish_2022-27)

After [the collapse of FTX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy_of_FTX "Bankruptcy of FTX") in late 2022, the movement underwent additional public scrutiny.[\[121\]](#cite_note-Wenar_2024-123)[\[138\]](#cite_note-Samuel_2022-140)[\[135\]](#cite_note-Tiku_2022-137)[\[139\]](#cite_note-141) Bankman-Fried's relationship with effective altruism damaged the movement's reputation.[\[26\]](#cite_note-Kulish_2022-27)[\[140\]](#cite_note-142) Some journalists asked whether the effective altruist movement was complicit in FTX's collapse, because it was convenient for leaders to overlook specific warnings about Bankman-Fried's behavior or questionable ethics at the trading firm Alameda.[\[120\]](#cite_note-Lewis-Kraus_2022a-122)[\[141\]](#cite_note-143) _[Fortune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_\(magazine\) "Fortune (magazine)")'_s crypto editor Jeff John Roberts said that "Bankman-Fried and his cronies professed devotion to 'EA,' but all their high-minded words turned out to be flimflam to justify robbing people".[\[142\]](#cite_note-Roberts_2023-144) MacAskill condemned Bankman-Fried's actions, saying that effective altruism emphasizes integrity.[\[138\]](#cite_note-Samuel_2022-140)[\[143\]](#cite_note-145) Philosopher [Leif Wenar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leif_Wenar "Leif Wenar") argued that Bankman-Fried's conduct typified much of the movement by focusing on positive impacts and [expected value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value "Expected value") without adequately weighing [risk and harm from philanthropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philanthropy#Criticism "Philanthropy"). He argued that the FTX case is not separable, as some in the EA community maintained, from the assumptions and reasoning that molded effective altruism as a philosophy in the first place—assumptions and reasoning that Wenar considered to be simplistic.[\[121\]](#cite_note-Wenar_2024-123)

### Sexual misconduct accusations

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Effective_altruism&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Sexual misconduct accusations")\]

Critiques also arose concerning issues of exclusion and [sexual harassment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_harassment "Sexual harassment").[\[144\]](#cite_note-Alter_2023-146)[\[145\]](#cite_note-147) A 2023 Bloomberg article featured some members of the effective altruism community who alleged that the philosophy masked a culture of predatory behavior.[\[146\]](#cite_note-148) In a 2023 _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_\(magazine\) "Time (magazine)")_ magazine article, seven women reported misconduct and controversy in the effective altruism movement. They accused men within the movement, typically in the [San Francisco Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area"), of using their power to groom younger women for [polyamorous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyamorous "Polyamorous") sexual relationships.[\[144\]](#cite_note-Alter_2023-146) The accusers argued that the majority male demographic and the polyamorous subculture combined to create an environment where sexual misconduct was tolerated, excused or rationalized away.[\[144\]](#cite_note-Alter_2023-146) In response to the accusations, the [Centre for Effective Altruism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Effective_Altruism "Centre for Effective Altruism") told _Time_ that some of the alleged perpetrators had already been banned from the organization and said it would investigate new claims.[\[144\]](#cite_note-Alter_2023-146) The organization also argued that it is challenging to discern to what extent sexual misconduct issues were specific to the effective altruism community or reflective of broader societal [misogyny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misogyny "Misogyny").[\[144\]](#cite_note-Alter_2023-146)

[Sam Altman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Altman "Sam Altman"), the CEO of OpenAI, has called effective altruism an "incredibly flawed movement" that shows "very weird emergent behavior".[\[147\]](#cite_note-McMillan_2023-149)\[_[further explanation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_\] Effective altruist concerns about AI risk were present among the OpenAI board members who fired Altman in November 2023;[\[142\]](#cite_note-Roberts_2023-144)[\[147\]](#cite_note-McMillan_2023-149)[\[148\]](#cite_note-150) he has since been reinstated as CEO and the Board membership has changed.[\[149\]](#cite_note-151)

[Timnit Gebru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timnit_Gebru "Timnit Gebru") and [Émile P. Torres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Émile_P._Torres "Émile P. Torres") argue that the effective altruism movement belongs to a network of interconnected movements they've termed [TESCREAL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TESCREAL "TESCREAL"), which they contend serves as intellectual justification for wealthy donors to shape humanity's future.[\[150\]](#cite_note-152) Gebru has also claimed that effective altruism has acted to overrule any other concerns regarding [AI ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_ethics "AI ethics") (e.g. [deepfake porn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepfake_pornography "Deepfake pornography"), [algorithmic bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithmic_bias "Algorithmic bias")), in the name of either preventing or [controlling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment "AI alignment") [artificial general intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_general_intelligence "Artificial general intelligence").[\[151\]](#cite_note-153)

The **Centre for Effective Altruism** (**CEA**) is an Oxford-based organisation that builds and supports the [effective altruism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_altruism "Effective altruism") community. It was founded in 2012 by [William MacAskill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_MacAskill "William MacAskill") and [Toby Ord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Ord "Toby Ord"), both philosophers at the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford").[\[1\]](#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](#cite_note-:1-2) CEA is part of Effective Ventures, a federation of effective altruism projects.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

CEA's founding was prompted by the need to set up an umbrella organization under which [Giving What We Can](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giving_What_We_Can "Giving What We Can") and [80,000 Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/80,000_Hours "80,000 Hours") could be incorporated.[\[2\]](#cite_note-:1-2) In late 2011, the members of those two organizations met to discuss how this new entity should be named, and the name "Centre for Effective Altruism" was adopted. At the time, the movement that would later be called "[effective altruism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_altruism "Effective altruism")" did not yet have a standard name—this was the first use of the term in its current sense.[\[4\]](#cite_note-:2-4)[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) CEA was registered as a charity the following year.[\[2\]](#cite_note-:1-2)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/William_MacAskill_Portrait_2015_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-William_MacAskill_Portrait_2015_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:William_MacAskill_Portrait_2015_\(cropped\).jpg)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Toby_Ord.jpg/250px-Toby_Ord.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Toby_Ord.jpg)

In 2015 and 2016, CEA incorporated several projects, including [Effective Altruism Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_Altruism_Global "Effective Altruism Global") and Giving What We Can, and began to function as a centralized organization, rather than merely as an umbrella. [Sam Bankman-Fried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Bankman-Fried "Sam Bankman-Fried") joined CEA as director of development in late 2017, leaving shortly thereafter to fund [Alameda Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alameda_Research "Alameda Research").[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) In 2018, CEA launched a new version of the Effective Altruism Forum, based on the [LessWrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LessWrong "LessWrong") codebase.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)

In 2022, the division of CEA providing operations support and fiscal sponsorship to several projects changed its name to "Effective Ventures".[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) The rest of CEA now operates as one of Effective Ventures’ many projects, which besides Giving What We Can and 80,000 Hours, include EA Funds, the Forethought Foundation, the Centre for the Governance of AI, Longview Philanthropy, Asterisk, Atlas Fellowship, and Non-trivial.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) CEA continues to pursue its mission to build and nurture a global community of people who are thinking carefully about the world's biggest problems and taking impactful action to solve them.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)

In 2022, the Centre for Effective Altruism launched and fiscally sponsored _Asterisk_, a quarterly magazine.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12)

As of 2022, CEA's primary activities include organizing the [Effective Altruism Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_Altruism_Global "Effective Altruism Global") conference series;[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) building and maintaining the Effective Altruism Forum and the effective altruism landing page;[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) funding and advising hundreds of effective altruism groups across the world.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)

CEA's offices are in Trajan House, a building that also accommodates many other organizations connected with the effective altruism movement, including the Forethought Foundation, the Centre for the Governance of AI, the Global Challenges Project, and the [Global Priorities Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Priorities_Institute "Global Priorities Institute"); the latter is also part of the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford").[\[4\]](#cite_note-:2-4)[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

CEA's budget for the year 2021 was $28 million.[\[2\]](#cite_note-:1-2)

## Research findings (background — not a source)
The claim is overstated and misleading. Yudkowsky is a major influence on the rationalist community and early AI-risk thinking, and the communities overlap. But there is no evidence that EA or its AI safety efforts are 'directly beholden' to him.

EA's origins are multiple and not mainly Yudkowsky's.
- Wikipedia says that in the later 2000s several communities converged: the GiveWell-centred evidence-based charity community (including Open Philanthropy), the Singularity Institute/MIRI, the Future of Humanity Institute, and the LessWrong rationalist forum. It names Peter Singer, Toby Ord and William MacAskill as influential philosophers. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effective_altruism
- Oxford philosophers founded the core EA organizations. Giving What We Can was founded at Oxford in 2009 by philosophers Toby Ord and William MacAskill. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giving_What_We_Can
- The Centre for Effective Altruism was founded in 2012 by Ord and MacAskill, both philosophers at the University of Oxford. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Effective_Altruism
- The EA Forum history says Ord's arguments, inspired by Singer's, led him to form Giving What We Can. https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/topics/history-of-effective-altruism

The sources show that EA's institutions have their own leadership and a separate lineage. They don't show that EA's AI safety work is directed by Yudkowsky. The convergence of communities means there is overlap and influence, not control. I did not find sources on Open Philanthropy's grantmaking or on EA researchers' differing views of Yudkowsky. Those points, and the Bay Area overlap claim, are unverified here.

Support for influence and overlap:
- Wikipedia's page on the rationalist community lists effective altruism and AI safety as heavily overlapping communities: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationalist_community

- A Substack essay says EAs are heavily influenced by the rationalist community that formed around Yudkowsky's Sequences: https://thingofthings.substack.com/p/effective-altruism-rationalist-epistemics
- The LessWrong description of the Sequences, quoted at https://www.aipanic.news/p/the-rationality-trap, calls them formative for substantial parts of the effective altruist community.

Evidence against 'beholden' or 'not separate':
- The same Substack essay opens with a disclaimer that EA is a diverse movement and many effective altruists believe different things: https://thingofthings.substack.com/p/effective-altruism-rationalist-epistemics

- Wikipedia describes the rationalist community's borders as blurry and debated: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationalist_community

The claim is therefore misleading.
