# ‘Oreogate’ has parents picking sides over a kindergartner’s lunchbox

![](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/b569c3276b4bf1fe113f85a8abd5a506e823a64b560a5462728db36a5cd01277/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w594_h387%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fkiro_cox_articles_720%2Fc43ff006ac5873496bc04300141194cc.jpg)

(Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) Justin Sullivan

A chocolate sandwich cookie has become the center of a viral parenting showdown, real or not, dubbed "Oreogate."

Here's the setup.

A series of Instagram posts by [@ashleighjamz](https://www.instagram.com/ashleighjamz/?hl=en) supposedly shows a group chat between moms whose five-year-olds all attend the same school.

One mom, allegedly called Michelle, said her daughter Ava came home upset because another little girl had Oreos in her lunchbox.

"We don't allow that kind of thing at home," Michelle explained.

And then she made the leap that apparently launched a thousand comments.

She asked the other moms if they could agree not to send Oreos because the children might compare lunches and feel like they're missing out.

And that is when the group chat fireworks began.

"Respectfully, I'm not changing my daughter's lunch because your daughter wants an Oreo," another mom, Charlotte, said.

The group chat blew up again when the Oreos showed up the next day in someone's lunchbox.

Then another mom, Laura, texted.

"That's literally just life," she said.

Boom. Pass the popcorn.

Or, apparently, hide the Oreos.

## Mom in 'Oreogate' allegedly gets school involved

Michelle, the mom who requested no Oreos, allegedly got the school involved.

In the end, the school sent an email encouraging healthy eating but giving parents discretion over what they pack.

But online, the conversation about "Oreogate" is far from over.

Parents had a lot to debate, everything from food restrictions to boundaries.

Even Kylie Kelce shared her take on her podcast "Not Gonna Lie."

"I fully support the opportunity for parents to feed their kids whatever they feel is going to be the best choice for their kids," Kelce said. "That is entirely your business, but you can't bring your thoughts and feelings into somebody else's lunchbox. That's not for you. Get your nose out of their lunchbox."

### 'Oreogate' may be fake

There is some talk online that "Oreogate" may not have been a real mom-group meltdown at all. The posts have not been verified as actual conversations, and the music playing was reportedly generated by AI.

But Oreo did release a statement saying the company has nothing to do with this drama.

But here's the funny thing: even if the Oreo conversation itself was manufactured, the argument feels very real to parents.

# Viral ‘Oreogate’ mom drama was a paid AI ad and its creator won’t say if it was real

A viral Instagram saga about a mother trying to ban Oreos from her daughter’s kindergarten has been confirmed as a paid partnership with an AI company, but its creator has declined to say whether the messages were authentic.

The drama, dubbed “Oreogate,” was shared by Instagram creator ashleighjamz across 13 videos. The [first installment surpassed 10 million views](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DcMjhWyzFYX/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsi=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==) as parents, medical creators and brands weighed in on the increasingly bizarre dispute.

Each video presented screenshots from an alleged parent WhatsApp group, with the messages transformed into songs using AI music generator Suno.

The saga began when a mother named Michelle asked other parents to stop packing Oreos, chocolate and candy because her daughter Ava was not allowed to eat them and became upset after seeing another child with the cookies.

Other mothers refused, while the messages claimed Michelle complained to the school, searched children’s lunchboxes and requested that Ava be seated away from classmates eating Oreos. A later installment seemingly revealed that Ava had been trading her own snacks for the forbidden cookies.

Oreo even joined the conversation, writing on its [official Threads account](https://www.threads.com/@oreo/post/DcbwwrSGem_/oreo-gate-was-not-on-my-bingo-card/): “OREO-gate was NOT on my 2026 bingo card.”

## Suno confirms creator partnership behind Oreogate

Despite being widely discussed as a genuine parent-group dispute, every Oreogate caption included the hashtag #sunopartner.

Suno subsequently confirmed to [Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/oreogate-mom-drama-suno-ad-fake-2026-8) that @ashleighjamz is one of its paid creator partners. The company said it did not devise or control the Oreogate storyline.

“Our creator partners have the freedom to use Suno however they want,” a spokesperson said. Oreo also told the outlet it had no involvement in producing the series.

> View on Threads

However, ashleighjamz did not directly answer when asked whether the messages, parents and children featured in Oreogate were real.

The creator said she had deliberately “not been getting into the specifics” while so many people were following the story. According to Business Insider, she stopped responding after receiving additional questions.

Questions had already been raised about the account by internet-culture writer [Stephanie McNeal](https://stephaniemcneal.substack.com/p/do-you-care-if-the-viral-mom-drama), who noted it was less than a month old and contained only sponsored Suno videos.

Those posts follow a similar format, including alleged messages from a disastrous bachelorette trip, an ex-boss and a “delusional” friend, all converted into AI-generated songs. Suno has also been used to create [other viral songs that left listeners questioning their origins](https://www.dexerto.com/tiktok/viral-tiktok-song-i-run-confirmed-ai-its-been-removed-from-spotify-3284524/).

There is currently no confirmation that the Oreogate messages were fabricated. However, with its creator declining to verify them, it remains unclear whether the saga documented a real dispute, was inspired by one or was created entirely as sponsored entertainment.

# A mom complained about her daughter's classmate bringing cookies to school. Welcome to Oreo-gate.

It's a 2026 parenting story that was destined to go viral.

The tale came from a mom named Ashleigh, who told it via [Instagram Reels](https://www.instagram.com/p/DcMjhWyzFYX/). According to her, the drama went down in a group chat for her daughter's elementary school classroom. A fellow mom named Michelle had reached out to the group of parents to ask that they all stop sending Oreos in their children's lunches, because it made her daughter, Ava, too jealous.

"I just wondered if we could agree not to send things like Oreos, chocolate candy, etc. so the kids aren't comparing lunches?" Michelle asked.

Predictably, all hell broke loose. The story — which has [involved multiple updates](https://www.instagram.com/p/DcgI5s5zxFD/) — had all the elements of modern parenting that people argue about ad nauseam online. On one side, there's the "crunchy" mom Michelle, who is willing to "[snowplow](https://www.yahoo.com/lifestyle/snowplow-parenting-trend-affects-kids-200049765.html)" over everyone else's Oreo enjoyment to ensure her precious little child doesn't deal with any negative emotion. 

On the other side, there are the "normal" moms, who just want their kids to be able to enjoy their ultra-processed sugar in peace. And on the internet, everyone was quick to jump onto Ashleigh's (aka Team Oreo) side. They labeled Michelle as overly controlling, applauding Ava's quest for Oreos despite her mother's best efforts — and vowing to send the cookies with their own children to cheer her on.

"Feeling like we should all just go ahead and pack Oreos in our kids lunches this week," wrote one kids food influencer on [Threads](https://www.threads.com/@bea_backett/post/DcdxbbwjiaH?hl=en). Pediatric nutrition experts [also waded in](https://www.instagram.com/p/DccWx5zpMSq/).

And of course, Oreo itself soon got wind of the tale. "OREO-gate was NOT on my 2026 bingo card," [wrote the brand](https://www.threads.com/@oreo/post/DcbwwrSGem_?hl=en).

The drama is so juicy, the discourse so hot and the virtue signaling so satisfying. Does it matter if anything about Oreo-gate is real? 

Because there are lots of reasons to be skeptical of "Ashleigh's" story. The account, [@AshleighJamz](https://www.instagram.com/ashleighjamz/) on Instagram, seems to exist for the sole purpose of turning alleged text-based drama from her life into silly songs using the AI song generator app Suno, which the account's creator lists as a "partner." 

Curiously, this isn't the first time "Ashleigh" has seen people throw down in the group chat. In fact, that's all she posts about. The account, which was created less than a month ago, also features videos about [workplace](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DbrjJsfTVpp/) drama, [bachelorette party](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DcHfGtPTVP_/) drama and [dating](https://www.instagram.com/reel/Db1-KWhTs6s/) drama — all of which are shown via group chats set to songs made using Suno. In fact, the account has never posted about anything else, and has tagged every post #SunoPartner.

I reached out to Suno to ask what the partnership between "Ashleigh" and the company entails, but a representative for the company said they did not have "anything to add" about the story, and would not confirm that the user behind the account had an active brand deal with the company. I also reached out via Instagram DM to "Ashleigh," but did not hear back. 

But if it is a planted or manufactured saga, whoever crafted it knew what they were doing. As Pamela Rutledge, the director of the [Media Psychology Research Center](https://mprcenter.org/about/pamela-rutledge/), tells me, the story was internet gold.

"Oreo-gate has all the trappings of good viral content: low stakes, high relatability, escalating conflict and emotion, identifiable heroes and villains, humor and episodic suspense," she says. "Each installment raises the stakes just enough to make people wait for the next episode. The AI songs enhance entertainment value and shareability. It also invites moral judgment that encourages comments, sharing and identification with a side. The cookie becomes incidental."

And of course, parents aren't jumping to weigh in because they feel the need to defend the honor of the esteemed Oreo. It's all about telegraphing the type of parent they want to be, or want to be seen as. As Rutledge puts it, the drama turns a lunchbox dispute into a "battle over parenting identity."

"Oreo-gate resonates because it hits several current parental hot buttons into one entertainingly ridiculous dispute that turns ordinary, relatable conflict into public entertainment: food restriction, parental control, children's autonomy, social comparison, school boundaries and parent-group politics and backchannelling," she says.

As she notes, debate over food restrictions in school, especially when it comes to allergies or concerns over nutritional value, has become a huge talking point both in real-world and online parenting spaces.

"When it's not a school-wide rule, one person expecting others to follow her rules challenges people's parental autonomy," Rutledge says. "Michelle is acting as a community voice, but she is one parent. Other parents push back against her assumption of compliance."

In that sense, whether Michelle and Ava exist is essentially irrelevant. The value that online commenters get comes from the performance of publicly acting out their values, telegraphing to others where they stand and, ultimately, what kind of parent they are. In other words, those invested in Oreo-gate don't care so much if the child they are cheering on to get her Oreos is actually real — just that everyone knows what they'd do if she were.

Should we be concerned that these blatantly fishy stories are causing this level of internet drama? Yes, but it makes sense once you understand that Ava and her Oreo were never the most important characters in the story. The discourse was.

# Viral ‘Oreogate’ mom drama was a paid AI ad and its creator won’t say if it was real

A viral Instagram saga about a mother trying to ban Oreos from her daughter’s kindergarten has been confirmed as a paid partnership with an AI company, but its creator has declined to say whether the messages were authentic.

The drama, dubbed “Oreogate,” was shared by Instagram creator ashleighjamz across 13 videos. The [first installment surpassed 10 million views](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DcMjhWyzFYX/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsi=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==) as parents, medical creators and brands weighed in on the increasingly bizarre dispute.

Each video presented screenshots from an alleged parent WhatsApp group, with the messages transformed into songs using AI music generator Suno.

The saga began when a mother named Michelle asked other parents to stop packing Oreos, chocolate and candy because her daughter Ava was not allowed to eat them and became upset after seeing another child with the cookies.

Other mothers refused, while the messages claimed Michelle complained to the school, searched children’s lunchboxes and requested that Ava be seated away from classmates eating Oreos. A later installment seemingly revealed that Ava had been trading her own snacks for the forbidden cookies.

Oreo even joined the conversation, writing on its [official Threads account](https://www.threads.com/@oreo/post/DcbwwrSGem_/oreo-gate-was-not-on-my-bingo-card/): “OREO-gate was NOT on my 2026 bingo card.”

## Suno confirms creator partnership behind Oreogate

Despite being widely discussed as a genuine parent-group dispute, every Oreogate caption included the hashtag #sunopartner.

Suno subsequently confirmed to [Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/oreogate-mom-drama-suno-ad-fake-2026-8) that @ashleighjamz is one of its paid creator partners. The company said it did not devise or control the Oreogate storyline.

“Our creator partners have the freedom to use Suno however they want,” a spokesperson said. Oreo also told the outlet it had no involvement in producing the series.

> View on Threads

MAPS: The story is widely repeated as oral history/legend, most associated with Colombia, where "Benkos Bioho, a formerly enslaved man, escaped and built a Palenque village" and "Women in the community would use their cornrows to create 'maps' and pass on escape routes" https://caro.news/how-cornrows-may-have-helped-free-slaves-navigate . Summary of research notes: "Oral histories passed down through African and diasporic communities tell us that during the era of plantation slavery, cornrow patterns were used to communicate. Routes north. Directions to safe houses. There is no written colonial record of this and there would not be." https://byot.substack.com/p/the-hairstyle-that-crossed-an-ocean  and "The most documented example of cornrows used as communication comes from Colombia. Benkos Biohò was an enslaved king who escaped captivity and built San Basilio de Palenque, the oldest free African town in the Americas." https://byot.substack.com/p/the-hairstyle-that-crossed-an-ocean .

EVIDENCE GAP FOR U.S. / GENERIC CLAIM: "A Snopes investigation in 2022 found no documentary evidence for the practice specifically within the United States but historian Tiffany Gill noted clearly that the absence of documentation does not negate the oral histories." https://byot.substack.com/p/the-hairstyle-that-crossed-an-ocean . Similarly summarized as Snopes "found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages." https://griffinsandgingersnaps.com/were-cornrows-used-by-enslaved-people-to-escape-slavery/ . Presentation as settled fact for generic "runaway slaves" therefore overstates documentation.

FOOD/SEEDS: The seed-hiding tradition has stronger academic support, but it refers to smuggling rice/seed for survival and transplanting African rice knowledge, not simply storing snacks for escape. "The tradition of hiding seeds in cornrows before boarding the ships is referenced by Professor Judith Carney in Black Rice (Harvard University Press, 2001) and her peer-reviewed article With Grains in Her Hair (Slavery & Abolition, 2004)." https://byot.substack.com/p/the-hairstyle-that-crossed-an-ocean . Also: "There are rice varieties still being grown today in Suriname, South America, in Maroon communities descended from people who escaped slavery... each variety carries the name of the woman who carried it to freedom in her cornrows when she fled" documented by researcher Tinde van Andel in peer-reviewed study in Slavery & Abolition in 2023 https://byot.substack.com/p/the-hairstyle-that-crossed-an-ocean . Related literature notes: "African women braided their hair and hid rice seeds as well as other grains in cornrows" and "Mothers often braided the rice into their children's hair to have something to survive on while on the slave trips or escaping" https://face2faceafrica.com/article/how-african-slaves-used-hair-to-smuggle-grains-into-the-caribbean-a-hidden-survival-story (via search snippet) .

### https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/
# Did Braiding Maps in Cornrows Help Black Slaves Escape Slavery?

News

## Stories shared on social media claimed that Black slaves would create maps in cornrows to help others escape slavery in the South.

### Published March 12, 2022

Some stories have value, even if we as fact-checkers can’t verify their authenticity.

The legend of cornrows and braids hiding maps and messages to freedom is both an idealistic tale, and indicative of the very real resilience of slaves living under brutal circumstances. The story mirrors others that seek to show slaves’ ingenuity, like one that [claimed](https://content.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1606271,00.html%22) messages encoded in quilts helped slaves escape to freedom on the Underground Railroad.

In February 2022, the African American Art & More Facebook page published a post about how Black [slaves](https://www.snopes.com/ap/2020/06/18/juneteenth-marks-when-slaves-were-freed/) purportedly [passed](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/cornrows-maps-slaves/) along maps and other information in cornrows to help them escape to the North.

https://www.facebook.com/AfricanAmericanArt/posts/10158597472266451

The post reads:

> Happy Black History Month‼️‼️❤️??
> 
> Did you know Cornrows were used to help slaves escape slavery?
> 
> Slaves used cornrows to transfer information and create maps to the north.
> 
> Since slaves were not allowed to read or write they had to pass information through cornrows.
> 
> It is believed to have originated in Colombia, South America where Benkos Bioho, in the late 1500’s came up with the idea to have women create maps & deliver messages through their cornrows. They were also called “canerows” to represent the sugarcane fields that slaves worked in.
> 
> One style had curved braids, tightly braided on their heads. The curved braids would represent the roads they would use to escape.
> 
> Also in their braids they kept gold and hid seeds which helped them survive after they escaped. They would use the seeds to plant crops once they were liberated.
> 
> Cornrows was the best way to not give back any suspicion to the owner. He would never figure out such a hairstyle would mean they would escape or the route they would take. #BlackHistoryMonth

One [copied](https://www.facebook.com/valerie.rice.5/posts/10219712235385737) version of the [post](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/cornrows-maps-slaves/) was shared more than 4,500 times. Several other posts with similar information information were shared at least hundreds of times each. We looked back and found that we had been receiving reader inquiries via email that asked about the subject since at least 2016. A reader also posted about this rumor in our [Snopes Tips Facebook group](https://www.facebook.com/groups/441333919315986/posts/4891477977634869/).

We read a number of accounts, and found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages. But this doesn’t mean that these stories should be disregarded, or that the practice never existed.

“When fugitive slaves figured out how to get themselves from place to place, they were incredibly brave and heroic people. That’s the core message and that's true,” Patricia Turner, folklorist and professor of African American studies at University of California Los Angeles, told us.

“\[These are\] kind of urban legends that \[serve a\] function of giving particulars to generalities. Slave messages on quilts and cornrows \[...\] make concrete \[or\] give a story to something that is ultimately very true in my mind,” she said.

Indeed, oral history in Colombia tells stories of Black slaves using their hair to convey messages. A 2011 [Washington Post](https://archive.ph/tCwtQ#selection-863.0-877.149) story about the Smithsonian Folklife Festival, detailed this history through [Ziomara Asprilla Garcia](https://festival.si.edu/2011/colombia/participant-portfolios/ziomara-asprilla-garcia/smithsonian), an Afro-Colombian hair braider:

> The first slaves arrived in Colombia around the beginning of the 16th century. Most were brought by the Spaniards who colonized the area. \[...\] But groups of slaves escaped and found refuge in areas that were geographically remote. In these areas, once thought to be uninhabitable, groups of runaway slaves thrived and built communities. The populations of these areas — including Choco, where Asprilla Garcia is from — have been mainly black for hundreds of years.
> 
> In the time of slavery in Colombia, hair braiding was used to relay messages. For example, to signal that they wanted to escape, women would braid a hairstyle called departes. “It had thick, tight braids, braided closely to the scalp and was tied into buns on the top,” Asprilla Garcia says.  
> \[...\]  
> “And another style had curved braids, tightly braided on their heads. The curved braids would represent the roads they would \[use to\] escape,” Asprilla Garcia says. “In the braids, they also kept gold and hid seeds which, in the long run, helped them survive after they escaped.”
> 
> “Why did they not speak the messages?” someone asks.
> 
> “By that time, a lot of the owners understood their language,” Asprilla Garcia says. The message in the women’s braids “was the best way to not give back any suspicion to owner. He would never figure out such a hairstyle would mean they would escape.”

The practice of hiding seeds in hair was mentioned in the book “[Black Rice: The African Origins of Rice Cultivation in the Americas](https://books.google.com.pr/books?id=YXWkwXHFWf0C&printsec=frontcover&dq=%22The+African+Origins+of+Rice+Cultivation+in+the+Americas%22&hl=en&sa=X&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q=hair&f=false),” by Judith Carney, a professor of geography at UCLA. She wrote about the possible African origins of a rice found in the South American country of Suriname:

> The centrality of rice for cultural identity in maroon history is also captured in legends recounted by their descendants, who claim their ancestors introduced the crop from Africa. In the area of Cayenne where a French agronomist found the Baga varieties, the Djuka maroons maintain that rice originally came from Africa, brought by female slaves who smuggled in their hair grains from the slave ships that transported them to the New World. If the legend is literally accurate, these must have been seed grains.  
> \[...\]  
> In studies of a separate maroon group, the Saramaka of Suriname, anthropologist Richard Price records a similar legend, where the presence of the crop is attributed to female ancestors’ hiding rice in their hair as they fled sugar plantations to freedom.

The use of hair to convey messages or hide grains of rice is so prevalent in oral retellings that the lack of documentation feels beside the point.

Even without proof of its authenticity, Turner says the practice made some sense in the U.S. “People felt Black bodies belonged to them. If \[Harriet Tubman\] had been searched there would have been no reservations about stripping her. The possibility that at some point someone may have hid something in their hair, I can't argue against \[...\] because it does adhere to some kind of logic at the time,” she said.

While there is not a lot of definitive research out there about cornrows, historians have been interrogating the myth of messages in quilts for a while. Numerous experts argued that such ideas were too fanciful a construction. Historian Fergus M. Bordewich wrote in a [New York Times](https://web.archive.org/web/20210317115330/https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/02/opinion/02bordewich.html) opinion piece in 2007:

> Few aspects of the American past have inspired more colorful mythology than the Underground Railroad. It’s probably fair to say that most Americans view it as a thrilling tapestry of midnight flights, hairbreadth escapes, mysterious codes and strange hiding places.
> 
> So it’s not surprising that the intriguing (if only recently invented) tale of escape maps encoded in antebellum quilts — enshrined in a metastasizing library of children’s books and teachers’ lesson plans and perhaps even in a Central Park memorial to Frederick Douglass — should also seize the popular imagination.

In her book, “[Crafted Lives: Stories and Studies of African-American Quilters](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Crafted_Lives_Stories_and_Studies_of_Afr/dfaPC_WSlNwC?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=railroad),” Turner interrogates the mythology around the quilts, and points out that they grew popular from children’s stories and oral history. In the 90s book, “Sweet Clara and the Freedom Quilt,” a young slave uses scraps of cloth to fashion a map on a quilt, something her master would never recognize.

We prodded Turner further on whether we could definitively answer the question posed in this article, but she preferred to focus on the attention that legends like this brought to the real stories of the resilience of Black slaves. “I am reticent to say anything too concrete, because I want lay people to want to know more about what life was like for enslaved people,” she responded. “There is no real value added to harshly saying “no” to a story.”

“You can couch your language \[and say\] ‘Well, no slave narrative covers it.’ Others will say, ‘Well that doesn’t mean it didn't happen,'" she continued.

And ultimately, stories are often told by people in positions of power, something that Turner believes the tales of the quilt and cornrows push back against. She said:

> One of the common denominators between the two stories is they focus on African Americans using their own resources for emancipation. If you look at stories that can be substantiated about the Underground Railroad, a lot of focus is on the white savior. The abolitionist or white conductor or Quaker, the parties that came in and helped the slaves, history gave a lot of attention \[to them\] as heroes. You could argue \[they got that attention\] because if ‘mainstream culture’ was white, and you depict white slave owners as evil, you want children to not have a negative view of white people. You make sure there are heroic white people too. At the end of the 20th century, Black people were telling the story and they were making the Black person the complete hero. You need narratives that reinforce the bravery of the Black people themselves. \[These stories\] come about at a time when talking about what Black people brought to the table was important politically, sociologically and economically.

While we cannot definitively answer the question of whether this was a real practice by slaves fleeing captivity in the American South, we can point to the rich and varied tales surrounding a real movement toward emancipation. Those stories certainly matter to people, hence their continuing popularity today.

**_Additional reporting by Jordan Liles._**

# Did slaves braid maps in cornrows to facilitate escape? History behind the legend

News

## Some stories have value, even if we as fact-checkers can’t verify their authenticity.

### Published May 16, 2026

For [years](https://x.com/centristpeater/status/2054691828826259922), a story that slaves' cornrows hid maps and messages to facilitate their escapes to freedom spread online as the stuff of internet legend. The idealistic story, indicative of the very real resilience of slaves living under brutal circumstances, mirrors others that seek to show slaves' ingenuity, like one that [claimed](https://content.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1606271,00.html) messages encoded in quilts helped slaves escape to freedom on the Underground Railroad. 

Examples of the claim appeared on [X](https://x.com/centristpeater/status/2054691828826259922) ([archived](https://perma.cc/STM9-QQC7)) and [Facebook.](https://www.facebook.com/photo/?fbid=122178080858200550&set=gm.8283090635117721&idorvanity=1305395626220625) One stated: 

> Cornrows were used during slavery to help slaves escape. Slaves used cornrows to transport and create maps to flee plantations. It is most documented in Colombia where Benkos Bioho, a king captured from Africa by the Portuguese who escaped slavery, built San Basillio de Palenque, a village in Northern Colombia around the 17th century. Bioho created his own language as well as an intelligence network and also came up with the idea to have women create maps and deliver messages through their cornrows.

![](https://mediaproxy.snopes.com/width/600?url=https://media.snopes.com/2026/05/cornrows_repack.png)

**(Facebook page Ancient Theories Nerd)**

Snopes has been receiving reader inquiries about the subject since at least 2016. A reader also posted about this rumor in our [Snopes Tips Facebook group](https://www.facebook.com/groups/441333919315986/posts/4891477977634869/).

We read a number of accounts, and found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages. But this doesn't mean that these stories should be disregarded, or that the practice never existed.

"When fugitive slaves figured out how to get themselves from place to place, they were incredibly brave and heroic people. That's the core message and that's true," Patricia Turner, folklorist and professor of African American studies at University of California, Los Angeles, told us.

"\[These are\] kind of urban legends that \[serve a\] function of giving particulars to generalities. Slave messages on quilts and cornrows ... make concrete \[or\] give a story to something that is ultimately very true in my mind," she said. 

Indeed, oral history in Colombia tells stories of Black slaves using their hair to convey messages. A 2011 [Washington Post](https://archive.ph/tCwtQ#selection-863.0-877.149) story about the Smithsonian Folklife Festival, detailed this history through [Ziomara Asprilla Garcia](https://festival.si.edu/2011/colombia/participant-portfolios/ziomara-asprilla-garcia/smithsonian), an Afro-Colombian hair braider:

> The first slaves arrived in Colombia around the beginning of the 16th century. Most were brought by the Spaniards who colonized the area. \[...\] But groups of slaves escaped and found refuge in areas that were geographically remote. In these areas, once thought to be uninhabitable, groups of runaway slaves thrived and built communities. The populations of these areas — including Choco, where Asprilla Garcia is from — have been mainly black for hundreds of years.
> 
> In the time of slavery in Colombia, hair braiding was used to relay messages. For example, to signal that they wanted to escape, women would braid a hairstyle called departes. "It had thick, tight braids, braided closely to the scalp and was tied into buns on the top," Asprilla Garcia says.  
> \[...\]  
> "And another style had curved braids, tightly braided on their heads. The curved braids would represent the roads they would \[use to\] escape," Asprilla Garcia says. "In the braids, they also kept gold and hid seeds which, in the long run, helped them survive after they escaped."
> 
> "Why did they not speak the messages?" someone asks.
> 
> "By that time, a lot of the owners understood their language," Asprilla Garcia says. The message in the women's braids "was the best way to not give back any suspicion to owner. He would never figure out such a hairstyle would mean they would escape."

The practice of hiding seeds in hair was mentioned in the book "[Black Rice: The African Origins of Rice Cultivation in the Americas](https://books.google.com.pr/books?id=YXWkwXHFWf0C&printsec=frontcover&dq=%22The+African+Origins+of+Rice+Cultivation+in+the+Americas%22&hl=en&sa=X&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q=hair&f=false)," by Judith Carney, a professor of geography at UCLA. She wrote about the possible African origins of a rice found in the South American country of Suriname:

> The centrality of rice for cultural identity in maroon history is also captured in legends recounted by their descendants, who claim their ancestors introduced the crop from Africa. In the area of Cayenne where a French agronomist found the Baga varieties, the Djuka maroons maintain that rice originally came from Africa, brought by female slaves who smuggled in their hair grains from the slave ships that transported them to the New World. If the legend is literally accurate, these must have been seed grains.   
> \[...\]  
> In studies of a separate maroon group, the Saramaka of Suriname, anthropologist Richard Price records a similar legend, where the presence of the crop is attributed to female ancestors' hiding rice in their hair as they fled sugar plantations to freedom. 

The use of hair to convey messages or hide grains of rice is so prevalent in oral retellings that the lack of documentation feels beside the point. 

Even without proof of its authenticity, Turner says the practice made some sense in the U.S. "People felt Black bodies belonged to them. If \[Harriet Tubman\] had been searched there would have been no reservations about stripping her. The possibility that at some point someone may have hid something in their hair, I can't argue against ... because it does adhere to some kind of logic at the time," she said. 

While there is not a lot of definitive research out there about cornrows, historians have been interrogating the myth of messages in quilts for a while. Numerous experts argued that such ideas were too fanciful a construction. Historian Fergus M. Bordewich wrote in a [New York Times](https://web.archive.org/web/20210317115330/https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/02/opinion/02bordewich.html) opinion piece in 2007:

> Few aspects of the American past have inspired more colorful mythology than the Underground Railroad. It's probably fair to say that most Americans view it as a thrilling tapestry of midnight flights, hairbreadth escapes, mysterious codes and strange hiding places.
> 
> So it's not surprising that the intriguing (if only recently invented) tale of escape maps encoded in antebellum quilts — enshrined in a metastasizing library of children's books and teachers' lesson plans and perhaps even in a Central Park memorial to Frederick Douglass — should also seize the popular imagination.

In her book, "[Crafted Lives: Stories and Studies of African-American Quilters](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Crafted_Lives_Stories_and_Studies_of_Afr/dfaPC_WSlNwC?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=railroad)," Turner interrogates the mythology around the quilts, and points out that they grew popular from children's stories and oral history. In the 90s book, "Sweet Clara and the Freedom Quilt," a young slave uses scraps of cloth to fashion a map on a quilt, something her master would never recognize. 

We prodded Turner further on whether we could definitively answer the question posed in this article, but she preferred to focus on the attention that legends like this brought to the real stories of the resilience of Black slaves. "I am reticent to say anything too concrete, because I want lay people to want to know more about what life was like for enslaved people," she responded. "There is no real value added to harshly saying 'no' to a story." 

"You can couch your language \[and say\] 'Well, no slave narrative covers it.' Others will say, 'Well that doesn't mean it didn't happen,'" she continued. 

And ultimately, stories are often told by people in positions of power, something that Turner believes the tales of the quilt and cornrows push back against. She said:

> One of the common denominators between the two stories is they focus on African Americans using their own resources for emancipation. If you look at stories that can be substantiated about the Underground Railroad, a lot of focus is on the white savior. The abolitionist or white conductor or Quaker, the parties that came in and helped the slaves, history gave a lot of attention \[to them\] as heroes. You could argue \[they got that attention\] because if 'mainstream culture' was white, and you depict white slave owners as evil, you want children to not have a negative view of white people. You make sure there are heroic white people too. At the end of the 20th century, Black people were telling the story and they were making the Black person the complete hero. You need narratives that reinforce the bravery of the Black people themselves. \[These stories\] come about at a time when talking about what Black people brought to the table was important politically, sociologically and economically.

While we cannot definitively answer the question of whether this was a real practice by slaves fleeing captivity in the American South, we can point to the rich and varied tales surrounding a real movement toward emancipation. Those stories certainly matter to people, hence their continuing popularity today. 

_Additional reporting by Jordan Liles._

“You can couch your language \[and say\] ‘Well, no slave narrative covers it.’ Others will say, ‘Well that doesn’t mean it didn't happen,'" she continued.

And ultimately, stories are often told by people in positions of power, something that Turner believes the tales of the quilt and cornrows push back against. She said:

> One of the common denominators between the two stories is they focus on African Americans using their own resources for emancipation. If you look at stories that can be substantiated about the Underground Railroad, a lot of focus is on the white savior. The abolitionist or white conductor or Quaker, the parties that came in and helped the slaves, history gave a lot of attention \[to them\] as heroes. You could argue \[they got that attention\] because if ‘mainstream culture’ was white, and you depict white slave owners as evil, you want children to not have a negative view of white people. You make sure there are heroic white people too. At the end of the 20th century, Black people were telling the story and they were making the Black person the complete hero. You need narratives that reinforce the bravery of the Black people themselves. \[These stories\] come about at a time when talking about what Black people brought to the table was important politically, sociologically and economically.

News

## Stories shared on social media claimed that Black slaves would create maps in cornrows to help others escape slavery in the South.

### Published March 12, 2022

Some stories have value, even if we as fact-checkers can’t verify their authenticity.

The legend of cornrows and braids hiding maps and messages to freedom is both an idealistic tale, and indicative of the very real resilience of slaves living under brutal circumstances. The story mirrors others that seek to show slaves’ ingenuity, like one that [claimed](https://content.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1606271,00.html%22) messages encoded in quilts helped slaves escape to freedom on the Underground Railroad.

In February 2022, the African American Art & More Facebook page published a post about how Black [slaves](https://www.snopes.com/ap/2020/06/18/juneteenth-marks-when-slaves-were-freed/) purportedly [passed](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/cornrows-maps-slaves/) along maps and other information in cornrows to help them escape to the North.

https://www.facebook.com/AfricanAmericanArt/posts/10158597472266451

The post reads:

> Happy Black History Month‼️‼️❤️??
> 
> Did you know Cornrows were used to help slaves escape slavery?
> 
> Slaves used cornrows to transfer information and create maps to the north.
> 
> Since slaves were not allowed to read or write they had to pass information through cornrows.
> 
> It is believed to have originated in Colombia, South America where Benkos Bioho, in the late 1500’s came up with the idea to have women create maps & deliver messages through their cornrows. They were also called “canerows” to represent the sugarcane fields that slaves worked in.
> 
> One style had curved braids, tightly braided on their heads. The curved braids would represent the roads they would use to escape.
> 
> Also in their braids they kept gold and hid seeds which helped them survive after they escaped. They would use the seeds to plant crops once they were liberated.
> 
> Cornrows was the best way to not give back any suspicion to the owner. He would never figure out such a hairstyle would mean they would escape or the route they would take. #BlackHistoryMonth

One [copied](https://www.facebook.com/valerie.rice.5/posts/10219712235385737) version of the [post](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/cornrows-maps-slaves/) was shared more than 4,500 times. Several other posts with similar information information were shared at least hundreds of times each. We looked back and found that we had been receiving reader inquiries via email that asked about the subject since at least 2016. A reader also posted about this rumor in our [Snopes Tips Facebook group](https://www.facebook.com/groups/441333919315986/posts/4891477977634869/).

We read a number of accounts, and found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages. But this doesn’t mean that these stories should be disregarded, or that the practice never existed.

“When fugitive slaves figured out how to get themselves from place to place, they were incredibly brave and heroic people. That’s the core message and that's true,” Patricia Turner, folklorist and professor of African American studies at University of California Los Angeles, told us.

“\[These are\] kind of urban legends that \[serve a\] function of giving particulars to generalities. Slave messages on quilts and cornrows \[...\] make concrete \[or\] give a story to something that is ultimately very true in my mind,” she said.

Indeed, oral history in Colombia tells stories of Black slaves using their hair to convey messages. A 2011 [Washington Post](https://archive.ph/tCwtQ#selection-863.0-877.149) story about the Smithsonian Folklife Festival, detailed this history through [Ziomara Asprilla Garcia](https://festival.si.edu/2011/colombia/participant-portfolios/ziomara-asprilla-garcia/smithsonian), an Afro-Colombian hair braider:

> The first slaves arrived in Colombia around the beginning of the 16th century. Most were brought by the Spaniards who colonized the area. \[...\] But groups of slaves escaped and found refuge in areas that were geographically remote. In these areas, once thought to be uninhabitable, groups of runaway slaves thrived and built communities. The populations of these areas — including Choco, where Asprilla Garcia is from — have been mainly black for hundreds of years.
> 
> In the time of slavery in Colombia, hair braiding was used to relay messages. For example, to signal that they wanted to escape, women would braid a hairstyle called departes. “It had thick, tight braids, braided closely to the scalp and was tied into buns on the top,” Asprilla Garcia says.  
> \[...\]  
> “And another style had curved braids, tightly braided on their heads. The curved braids would represent the roads they would \[use to\] escape,” Asprilla Garcia says. “In the braids, they also kept gold and hid seeds which, in the long run, helped them survive after they escaped.”
> 
> “Why did they not speak the messages?” someone asks.
> 
> “By that time, a lot of the owners understood their language,” Asprilla Garcia says. The message in the women’s braids “was the best way to not give back any suspicion to owner. He would never figure out such a hairstyle would mean they would escape.”

> The centrality of rice for cultural identity in maroon history is also captured in legends recounted by their descendants, who claim their ancestors introduced the crop from Africa. If the legend is literally accurate, these must have been seed grains.  
> \[...\]  
> In studies of a separate maroon group, the Saramaka of Suriname, anthropologist Richard Price records a similar legend, where the presence of the crop is attributed to female ancestors’ hiding rice in their hair as they fled sugar plantations to freedom.

If \[Harriet Tubman\] had been searched there would have been no reservations about stripping her. # Did slaves braid maps in cornrows to facilitate escape? History behind the legend

News

## Some stories have value, even if we as fact-checkers can’t verify their authenticity.

### Published May 16, 2026

For [years](https://x.com/centristpeater/status/2054691828826259922), a story that slaves' cornrows hid maps and messages to facilitate their escapes to freedom spread online as the stuff of internet legend. The idealistic story, indicative of the very real resilience of slaves living under brutal circumstances, mirrors others that seek to show slaves' ingenuity, like one that [claimed](https://content.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1606271,00.html) messages encoded in quilts helped slaves escape to freedom on the Underground Railroad. 

Examples of the claim appeared on [X](https://x.com/centristpeater/status/2054691828826259922) ([archived](https://perma.cc/STM9-QQC7)) and [Facebook.](https://www.facebook.com/photo/?fbid=122178080858200550&set=gm.8283090635117721&idorvanity=1305395626220625) One stated: 

> Cornrows were used during slavery to help slaves escape. Slaves used cornrows to transport and create maps to flee plantations. It is most documented in Colombia where Benkos Bioho, a king captured from Africa by the Portuguese who escaped slavery, built San Basillio de Palenque, a village in Northern Colombia around the 17th century. Bioho created his own language as well as an intelligence network and also came up with the idea to have women create maps and deliver messages through their cornrows.

![](https://mediaproxy.snopes.com/width/600?url=https://media.snopes.com/2026/05/cornrows_repack.png)

**(Facebook page Ancient Theories Nerd)**

Snopes has been receiving reader inquiries about the subject since at least 2016. A reader also posted about this rumor in our [Snopes Tips Facebook group](https://www.facebook.com/groups/441333919315986/posts/4891477977634869/).

We read a number of accounts, and found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages. But this doesn't mean that these stories should be disregarded, or that the practice never existed.

"When fugitive slaves figured out how to get themselves from place to place, they were incredibly brave and heroic people. That's the core message and that's true," Patricia Turner, folklorist and professor of African American studies at University of California, Los Angeles, told us.

"\[These are\] kind of urban legends that \[serve a\] function of giving particulars to generalities. Slave messages on quilts and cornrows ... make concrete \[or\] give a story to something that is ultimately very true in my mind," she said. 

Indeed, oral history in Colombia tells stories of Black slaves using their hair to convey messages. A 2011 [Washington Post](https://archive.ph/tCwtQ#selection-863.0-877.149) story about the Smithsonian Folklife Festival, detailed this history through [Ziomara Asprilla Garcia](https://festival.si.edu/2011/colombia/participant-portfolios/ziomara-asprilla-garcia/smithsonian), an Afro-Colombian hair braider:

> The first slaves arrived in Colombia around the beginning of the 16th century. Most were brought by the Spaniards who colonized the area. \[...\] But groups of slaves escaped and found refuge in areas that were geographically remote. In these areas, once thought to be uninhabitable, groups of runaway slaves thrived and built communities. The populations of these areas — including Choco, where Asprilla Garcia is from — have been mainly black for hundreds of years.
> 
> In the time of slavery in Colombia, hair braiding was used to relay messages. For example, to signal that they wanted to escape, women would braid a hairstyle called departes. "It had thick, tight braids, braided closely to the scalp and was tied into buns on the top," Asprilla Garcia says.  
> \[...\]  
> "And another style had curved braids, tightly braided on their heads. The curved braids would represent the roads they would \[use to\] escape," Asprilla Garcia says. "In the braids, they also kept gold and hid seeds which, in the long run, helped them survive after they escaped."
> 
> "Why did they not speak the messages?" someone asks.
> 
> "By that time, a lot of the owners understood their language," Asprilla Garcia says. The message in the women's braids "was the best way to not give back any suspicion to owner. He would never figure out such a hairstyle would mean they would escape."

The practice of hiding seeds in hair was mentioned in the book "[Black Rice: The African Origins of Rice Cultivation in the Americas](https://books.google.com.pr/books?id=YXWkwXHFWf0C&printsec=frontcover&dq=%22The+African+Origins+of+Rice+Cultivation+in+the+Americas%22&hl=en&sa=X&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q=hair&f=false)," by Judith Carney, a professor of geography at UCLA. She wrote about the possible African origins of a rice found in the South American country of Suriname:

> The centrality of rice for cultural identity in maroon history is also captured in legends recounted by their descendants, who claim their ancestors introduced the crop from Africa. In the area of Cayenne where a French agronomist found the Baga varieties, the Djuka maroons maintain that rice originally came from Africa, brought by female slaves who smuggled in their hair grains from the slave ships that transported them to the New World. If the legend is literally accurate, these must have been seed grains.   
> \[...\]  
> In studies of a separate maroon group, the Saramaka of Suriname, anthropologist Richard Price records a similar legend, where the presence of the crop is attributed to female ancestors' hiding rice in their hair as they fled sugar plantations to freedom. 

The use of hair to convey messages or hide grains of rice is so prevalent in oral retellings that the lack of documentation feels beside the point. 

Even without proof of its authenticity, Turner says the practice made some sense in the U.S. "People felt Black bodies belonged to them. If \[Harriet Tubman\] had been searched there would have been no reservations about stripping her. The possibility that at some point someone may have hid something in their hair, I can't argue against ... because it does adhere to some kind of logic at the time," she said. 

While there is not a lot of definitive research out there about cornrows, historians have been interrogating the myth of messages in quilts for a while. Numerous experts argued that such ideas were too fanciful a construction. Historian Fergus M. Bordewich wrote in a [New York Times](https://web.archive.org/web/20210317115330/https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/02/opinion/02bordewich.html) opinion piece in 2007:

> Few aspects of the American past have inspired more colorful mythology than the Underground Railroad. It's probably fair to say that most Americans view it as a thrilling tapestry of midnight flights, hairbreadth escapes, mysterious codes and strange hiding places.
> 
> So it's not surprising that the intriguing (if only recently invented) tale of escape maps encoded in antebellum quilts — enshrined in a metastasizing library of children's books and teachers' lesson plans and perhaps even in a Central Park memorial to Frederick Douglass — should also seize the popular imagination.

In her book, "[Crafted Lives: Stories and Studies of African-American Quilters](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Crafted_Lives_Stories_and_Studies_of_Afr/dfaPC_WSlNwC?hl=en&gbpv=1&bsq=railroad)," Turner interrogates the mythology around the quilts, and points out that they grew popular from children's stories and oral history. In the 90s book, "Sweet Clara and the Freedom Quilt," a young slave uses scraps of cloth to fashion a map on a quilt, something her master would never recognize. 

We prodded Turner further on whether we could definitively answer the question posed in this article, but she preferred to focus on the attention that legends like this brought to the real stories of the resilience of Black slaves. "I am reticent to say anything too concrete, because I want lay people to want to know more about what life was like for enslaved people," she responded. "There is no real value added to harshly saying 'no' to a story." 

"You can couch your language \[and say\] 'Well, no slave narrative covers it.' Others will say, 'Well that doesn't mean it didn't happen,'" she continued. 

And ultimately, stories are often told by people in positions of power, something that Turner believes the tales of the quilt and cornrows push back against. She said:

> One of the common denominators between the two stories is they focus on African Americans using their own resources for emancipation. If you look at stories that can be substantiated about the Underground Railroad, a lot of focus is on the white savior. The abolitionist or white conductor or Quaker, the parties that came in and helped the slaves, history gave a lot of attention \[to them\] as heroes. You could argue \[they got that attention\] because if 'mainstream culture' was white, and you depict white slave owners as evil, you want children to not have a negative view of white people. You make sure there are heroic white people too. At the end of the 20th century, Black people were telling the story and they were making the Black person the complete hero. You need narratives that reinforce the bravery of the Black people themselves. \[These stories\] come about at a time when talking about what Black people brought to the table was important politically, sociologically and economically.

While we cannot definitively answer the question of whether this was a real practice by slaves fleeing captivity in the American South, we can point to the rich and varied tales surrounding a real movement toward emancipation. Those stories certainly matter to people, hence their continuing popularity today. 

_Additional reporting by Jordan Liles._

Most independent sources agree the claim originates as folklore primarily associated with Colombia/South America, not the U.S. South: "Most sources place the folk claims in countries outside the United States, primarily Colombia and South Africa" (https://www.truthorfiction.com/did-slaves-braid-routes-to-freedom-into-hairstyles/). Historians interviewed, such as folklorist Patricia Turner, describe these as 'urban legends' that serve to personalize broader historical truths about slave resilience, rather than verified documented practices (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/). Critics on social media and in forums have also pointed out practical problems with the 'hidden seeds/food' claim, comparing it to the debunked 'rice in hair' legend, noting seeds or food would likely rot from sweat during a journey, and that there is no verified documentation of this specific practice (https://www.lipstickalley.com/threads/slaves-used-cornrows-to-transfer-and-create-maps-to-leave-plantations.4570251/). In short, while the story is popular and emotionally resonant, it lacks solid historical documentation, especially regarding U.S. slavery, and is best described as an unverified legend rather than established fact.

### https://fortune.com/2023/06/09/mark-zuckerberg-elon-musk-twitter-meta-layoffs-middle-managers
# Zuckerberg credits Musk with kicking off tech trend of firing middle managers | Fortune

Mark Zuckerberg is giving credit where credit is due. The Meta CEO believes that Elon Musk, by firing hordes of middle managers at Twitter after his $44 billion takeover last October, kicked off a trend that’s been “good for the industry.” 

After assuming control, Musk laid off thousands of employees, reducing headcount from about 7,500 to less than 2,000 by February of this year, [according to](https://techcrunch.com/2023/05/25/elon-musk-twitter-everything-you-need-to-know/) TechCrunch.

Zuckerberg delivered the comments [on the _Lex Fridman Podcast_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ff4fRgnuFgQ) on Thursday. The way he sees it—and laid-off Twitter employees would surely beg to differ—Musk was right in trying to make the company “more technical” and decrease the distance between engineers and himself, with “fewer layers of management.” 

“His actions led me and I think a lot of other folks in the industry to think about, ‘Hey, are we kind of doing this as much as we should?’” he said. “Could we make our companies better by pushing on some of the same principles?…My sense is that there were a lot of other people who thought that those were good changes, but who may have been a little shy about doing them.” 

It was something Musk “was quite ahead of a bunch of the other companies on,” he added.

Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, [announced in March](https://fortune.com/2023/03/14/meta-layoffs-10000-mark-zuckerberg-year-of-efficiency-hiring-freeze/) that it would lay off 10,000 employees—adding to the 11,000 job cuts it started last November—and would also freeze hiring on 5,000 more positions. In a [blog post](https://about.fb.com/news/2023/03/mark-zuckerberg-meta-year-of-efficiency/), Zuckerberg said he would “make our organization flatter by removing multiple layers of management,” part of a “year of efficiency.”

While Meta employees have [described “shattered” morale](https://fortune.com/2023/04/20/meta-employees-tech-layoffs-mark-zuckerberg-morale-confidence/), Wall Street has responded positively, with Meta shares up about 112% year to date.

Other big tech companies have [also shed workers this year](https://fortune.com/2023/01/07/salesforce-ceo-marc-benioff-dodges-layoffs-questions-ohana-mantra-questioned/), among them [Salesforce](https://fortune.com/company/salesforce-com/), [Microsoft](https://fortune.com/company/microsoft/), and [Amazon](https://fortune.com/company/amazon-com/). Tech layoffs in 2023 are [the highest they’ve been](https://fortune.com/2023/06/01/tech-layoffs-worst-since-dot-com-bubble-burst/) since the dotcom bubble burst 22 years ago, according to a [report](https://www.challengergray.com/blog/may-2023-layoffs-jump-on-tech-retail-auto-ytd-hiring-lowest-since-2016/) released earlier this month by recruiting firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

Part of the problem was that many tech companies had simply over-hired in recent years, both because the pandemic increased demand for their products and services and because it was a period of easy money given Fed-induced low interest rates.

Stewart Butterfield, former CEO of Slack, recently [described a dynamic](https://fortune.com/2023/05/28/ex-slack-ceo-stewart-butterfield-tech-over-hiring-root-of-excess/) within tech companies behind much of the over-hiring. He noted on Bloomberg’s _Odd Lots_ [podcast](https://omny.fm/shows/odd-lots/slack-founder-stewart-butterfield-on-ai-software-a) in late May that when there’s no real constraint on hiring, “you hire someone, and the first thing that person wants to do is hire other people.” The reason is that “the more people who report to you, the higher your prestige, the more your power in the organization…So every budgeting process is, ‘I really want to hire,’ and that to me is the root of all the excess.”

Zuckerberg said it was “very hard to know” from the outside whether Musk fired too many or not enough workers at Twitter, but said the trend he helped kick-start “hopefully can be good for the industry and make all these companies more productive over time.”  

In May, Musk admitted that not all the employees he fired were superfluous. “Desperate times call for desperate measures,” he [told](https://twitter.com/CNBC/status/1658663628684533761) CNBC. “There’s no question that some of the people who were let go probably shouldn’t have been let go.”

He [told the BBC](https://fortune.com/2023/04/12/elon-musk-twitter-job-cuts-redundancies-layoffs-company-was-going-to-die/) in April that Twitter “was going to go bankrupt if we did not cut costs immediately. This is not a caring-uncaring situation: If the whole ship sinks, then nobody’s got a job.” Musk took on [billions in debt](https://fortune.com/2023/01/18/elon-musk-twitter-sales-revenue-interest-payment-loans-debt/) to finance his takeover, making the situation even more pressing. 

At Meta, Zuckerberg did not face the same kind of financial urgency. 

“It’s a kind of strategy decision and sometimes financially required, but not fully in our case,” he said. “A lot of it was more culturally and strategically driven by this push where I wanted us to become a stronger technology company.”

He explained that he wanted to “empower engineers more, the people who are building things, the technical teams,” and part of that was making sure those employees are “not the leaf nodes of the organization. I don’t want, like, eight levels of management and then the people actually doing the work.”

He added, “I think over time companies just build up very large support functions that are not doing the kind of core technical work, and those functions are very important, but I think having them in the right proportion is important.”

### https://fortune.com/2023/06/09/mark-zuckerberg-elon-musk-twitter-meta-layoffs-middle-managers/
# Zuckerberg credits Musk with kicking off tech trend of firing middle managers | Fortune

Mark Zuckerberg is giving credit where credit is due. The Meta CEO believes that Elon Musk, by firing hordes of middle managers at Twitter after his $44 billion takeover last October, kicked off a trend that’s been “good for the industry.” 

After assuming control, Musk laid off thousands of employees, reducing headcount from about 7,500 to less than 2,000 by February of this year, [according to](https://techcrunch.com/2023/05/25/elon-musk-twitter-everything-you-need-to-know/) TechCrunch.

Zuckerberg delivered the comments [on the _Lex Fridman Podcast_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ff4fRgnuFgQ) on Thursday. The way he sees it—and laid-off Twitter employees would surely beg to differ—Musk was right in trying to make the company “more technical” and decrease the distance between engineers and himself, with “fewer layers of management.” 

“His actions led me and I think a lot of other folks in the industry to think about, ‘Hey, are we kind of doing this as much as we should?’” he said. “Could we make our companies better by pushing on some of the same principles?…My sense is that there were a lot of other people who thought that those were good changes, but who may have been a little shy about doing them.” 

It was something Musk “was quite ahead of a bunch of the other companies on,” he added.

Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, [announced in March](https://fortune.com/2023/03/14/meta-layoffs-10000-mark-zuckerberg-year-of-efficiency-hiring-freeze/) that it would lay off 10,000 employees—adding to the 11,000 job cuts it started last November—and would also freeze hiring on 5,000 more positions. In a [blog post](https://about.fb.com/news/2023/03/mark-zuckerberg-meta-year-of-efficiency/), Zuckerberg said he would “make our organization flatter by removing multiple layers of management,” part of a “year of efficiency.”

While Meta employees have [described “shattered” morale](https://fortune.com/2023/04/20/meta-employees-tech-layoffs-mark-zuckerberg-morale-confidence/), Wall Street has responded positively, with Meta shares up about 112% year to date.

Other big tech companies have [also shed workers this year](https://fortune.com/2023/01/07/salesforce-ceo-marc-benioff-dodges-layoffs-questions-ohana-mantra-questioned/), among them [Salesforce](https://fortune.com/company/salesforce-com/), [Microsoft](https://fortune.com/company/microsoft/), and [Amazon](https://fortune.com/company/amazon-com/). Tech layoffs in 2023 are [the highest they’ve been](https://fortune.com/2023/06/01/tech-layoffs-worst-since-dot-com-bubble-burst/) since the dotcom bubble burst 22 years ago, according to a [report](https://www.challengergray.com/blog/may-2023-layoffs-jump-on-tech-retail-auto-ytd-hiring-lowest-since-2016/) released earlier this month by recruiting firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

Part of the problem was that many tech companies had simply over-hired in recent years, both because the pandemic increased demand for their products and services and because it was a period of easy money given Fed-induced low interest rates.

Stewart Butterfield, former CEO of Slack, recently [described a dynamic](https://fortune.com/2023/05/28/ex-slack-ceo-stewart-butterfield-tech-over-hiring-root-of-excess/) within tech companies behind much of the over-hiring. He noted on Bloomberg’s _Odd Lots_ [podcast](https://omny.fm/shows/odd-lots/slack-founder-stewart-butterfield-on-ai-software-a) in late May that when there’s no real constraint on hiring, “you hire someone, and the first thing that person wants to do is hire other people.” The reason is that “the more people who report to you, the higher your prestige, the more your power in the organization…So every budgeting process is, ‘I really want to hire,’ and that to me is the root of all the excess.”

Zuckerberg said it was “very hard to know” from the outside whether Musk fired too many or not enough workers at Twitter, but said the trend he helped kick-start “hopefully can be good for the industry and make all these companies more productive over time.”  

In May, Musk admitted that not all the employees he fired were superfluous. “Desperate times call for desperate measures,” he [told](https://twitter.com/CNBC/status/1658663628684533761) CNBC. “There’s no question that some of the people who were let go probably shouldn’t have been let go.”

He [told the BBC](https://fortune.com/2023/04/12/elon-musk-twitter-job-cuts-redundancies-layoffs-company-was-going-to-die/) in April that Twitter “was going to go bankrupt if we did not cut costs immediately. This is not a caring-uncaring situation: If the whole ship sinks, then nobody’s got a job.” Musk took on [billions in debt](https://fortune.com/2023/01/18/elon-musk-twitter-sales-revenue-interest-payment-loans-debt/) to finance his takeover, making the situation even more pressing. 

At Meta, Zuckerberg did not face the same kind of financial urgency. 

“It’s a kind of strategy decision and sometimes financially required, but not fully in our case,” he said. “A lot of it was more culturally and strategically driven by this push where I wanted us to become a stronger technology company.”

He explained that he wanted to “empower engineers more, the people who are building things, the technical teams,” and part of that was making sure those employees are “not the leaf nodes of the organization. I don’t want, like, eight levels of management and then the people actually doing the work.”

He added, “I think over time companies just build up very large support functions that are not doing the kind of core technical work, and those functions are very important, but I think having them in the right proportion is important.”

# Zuckerberg credits Musk with kicking off tech trend of firing middle managers | Fortune

Mark Zuckerberg is giving credit where credit is due. The Meta CEO believes that Elon Musk, by firing hordes of middle managers at Twitter after his $44 billion takeover last October, kicked off a trend that’s been “good for the industry.” 

After assuming control, Musk laid off thousands of employees, reducing headcount from about 7,500 to less than 2,000 by February of this year, [according to](https://techcrunch.com/2023/05/25/elon-musk-twitter-everything-you-need-to-know/) TechCrunch.

Zuckerberg delivered the comments [on the _Lex Fridman Podcast_](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ff4fRgnuFgQ) on Thursday. The way he sees it—and laid-off Twitter employees would surely beg to differ—Musk was right in trying to make the company “more technical” and decrease the distance between engineers and himself, with “fewer layers of management.” 

“His actions led me and I think a lot of other folks in the industry to think about, ‘Hey, are we kind of doing this as much as we should?’” he said. “Could we make our companies better by pushing on some of the same principles?…My sense is that there were a lot of other people who thought that those were good changes, but who may have been a little shy about doing them.” 

It was something Musk “was quite ahead of a bunch of the other companies on,” he added.

Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, [announced in March](https://fortune.com/2023/03/14/meta-layoffs-10000-mark-zuckerberg-year-of-efficiency-hiring-freeze/) that it would lay off 10,000 employees—adding to the 11,000 job cuts it started last November—and would also freeze hiring on 5,000 more positions. In a [blog post](https://about.fb.com/news/2023/03/mark-zuckerberg-meta-year-of-efficiency/), Zuckerberg said he would “make our organization flatter by removing multiple layers of management,” part of a “year of efficiency.”

While Meta employees have [described “shattered” morale](https://fortune.com/2023/04/20/meta-employees-tech-layoffs-mark-zuckerberg-morale-confidence/), Wall Street has responded positively, with Meta shares up about 112% year to date.

Other big tech companies have [also shed workers this year](https://fortune.com/2023/01/07/salesforce-ceo-marc-benioff-dodges-layoffs-questions-ohana-mantra-questioned/), among them [Salesforce](https://fortune.com/company/salesforce-com/), [Microsoft](https://fortune.com/company/microsoft/), and [Amazon](https://fortune.com/company/amazon-com/). Tech layoffs in 2023 are [the highest they’ve been](https://fortune.com/2023/06/01/tech-layoffs-worst-since-dot-com-bubble-burst/) since the dotcom bubble burst 22 years ago, according to a [report](https://www.challengergray.com/blog/may-2023-layoffs-jump-on-tech-retail-auto-ytd-hiring-lowest-since-2016/) released earlier this month by recruiting firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

Part of the problem was that many tech companies had simply over-hired in recent years, both because the pandemic increased demand for their products and services and because it was a period of easy money given Fed-induced low interest rates.

Stewart Butterfield, former CEO of Slack, recently [described a dynamic](https://fortune.com/2023/05/28/ex-slack-ceo-stewart-butterfield-tech-over-hiring-root-of-excess/) within tech companies behind much of the over-hiring. He noted on Bloomberg’s _Odd Lots_ [podcast](https://omny.fm/shows/odd-lots/slack-founder-stewart-butterfield-on-ai-software-a) in late May that when there’s no real constraint on hiring, “you hire someone, and the first thing that person wants to do is hire other people.” The reason is that “the more people who report to you, the higher your prestige, the more your power in the organization…So every budgeting process is, ‘I really want to hire,’ and that to me is the root of all the excess.”

Zuckerberg said it was “very hard to know” from the outside whether Musk fired too many or not enough workers at Twitter, but said the trend he helped kick-start “hopefully can be good for the industry and make all these companies more productive over time.”  

In May, Musk admitted that not all the employees he fired were superfluous. “Desperate times call for desperate measures,” he [told](https://twitter.com/CNBC/status/1658663628684533761) CNBC. “There’s no question that some of the people who were let go probably shouldn’t have been let go.”

He [told the BBC](https://fortune.com/2023/04/12/elon-musk-twitter-job-cuts-redundancies-layoffs-company-was-going-to-die/) in April that Twitter “was going to go bankrupt if we did not cut costs immediately. This is not a caring-uncaring situation: If the whole ship sinks, then nobody’s got a job.” Musk took on [billions in debt](https://fortune.com/2023/01/18/elon-musk-twitter-sales-revenue-interest-payment-loans-debt/) to finance his takeover, making the situation even more pressing. 

At Meta, Zuckerberg did not face the same kind of financial urgency. 

“It’s a kind of strategy decision and sometimes financially required, but not fully in our case,” he said. “A lot of it was more culturally and strategically driven by this push where I wanted us to become a stronger technology company.”

He explained that he wanted to “empower engineers more, the people who are building things, the technical teams,” and part of that was making sure those employees are “not the leaf nodes of the organization. I don’t want, like, eight levels of management and then the people actually doing the work.”

He added, “I think over time companies just build up very large support functions that are not doing the kind of core technical work, and those functions are very important, but I think having them in the right proportion is important.”
